speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: GOOSE BAY STATION
subsubtopic: LEASE OF LAND TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I beg leave to table copies of notes exchanged by the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs and the United States ambassador on December 5. The notes constitute a lease to the United States of certain parcels of land within the Royal Canadian Air Force station at Goose Bay in the province of Newfoundland. The lease, which is to enable the United States air force to replace wartime construction and to construct some additional facilities, involves approximately 7,000 acres of land which is less than ten per cent of the area of the base. The field will continue to be under the over-all command of the R.C.A.F.
Goose Bay airport was built by Canada in 1942-before Newfoundland entered confederation-as a stepping-stone along the North Atlantic and Arctic airways. During the war thousands of aircraft put down there on ferry flights from the United States and Canada to Europe. Since the war Goose Bay has been used by the R.C.A.F. and the United States air force to support certain northern weather stations, and it has served also as a centre for search and rescue operations in the area.
In view of the increased international tension during the last three years, the R.C.A.F. and United States air force facilities at Goose Bay have been considerably expanded. The base is, in effect, a joint defence installation, and is being used by both air forces for the co-operative defence of North America. Its use by both countries is essential for the fulfilment of their responsibilities under the North Atlantic treaty.
The lease is for a period of 20 years, with the proviso that any United States request for an extension will be considered by Canada in the light of the common defence interests of Canada and the United States.
When the lease has expired, all buildings on the leased area will become the property of Canada, but removable improvements may be taken away by the United States air force.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked me whether I could inform the house as to the incident which occurred at Chalk River on Friday last. I can now report as follows:
About 3.15 on Friday afternoon, December 12, a burst occurred in uranium rods during a normal operation. The release of radioactive gases and dust from the rods was carried as usual by the ventilating system up the tall stack from which it would normally be widely dispersed. Owing to the atmospheric conditions at the time and the severity of the discharge, the area of the plant became contaminated causing the alarms to go off and the "stay-in" signals were at once given. The activity at the remote buildings died off in a matter of some minutes but the health surveyors found activity remaining in the laboratories nearer the pile building and to avoid the spread of contamination which would affect the research instruments and laboratories by people walking around, it was decided to evacuate all personnel who were not essential to operation. The evacuation siren was sounded and all employees, except the scientists and engineers attending the reactor, and all senior officers, left the plant in a very orderly fashion, without panic and according to the procedures set down for such emergencies. No one was hurt or injured by contamination, though the clothes of a few men in the pile building were removed as a precautionary measure until the short-lived activity on them died down. I am informed, however, that it will take several days to clear all the laboratories of contamination which,


although well below the level standard for human tolerance, does seriously interfere with scientific instruments and experiments.
Bursts of rods have occurred before at Chalk River but this one was more severe and atmospheric conditions were such as to reduce the dispersion. Bursts have occurred at other atomic energy plants, and must be expected when scientists are dealing with such a powerful source of energy of a new type and have still much to learn about the behaviour of materials under high irradiation. The metallurgical changes which may be produced by such powerful neutron bombardment is one problem on which scientists are still working.
The reactor is now being cooled off to permit the engineers and scientists to undertake a complete examination, discover the real trouble and make any necessary repairs. In the meantime, however, all scientific, maintenance and operating personnel are now back to work and fully occupied.
It should be remembered that NRX is an experimental plant designed during the war when there was little if any operating experience and, as in all novel development work, it is from the troubles met in experimental establishments that enough experience is gained to design large-scale industrial plants.

subtopic: DAMAGE AT CHALK RIVER PLANT
speechtext: Will the reactor be out of operation for some time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DAMAGE AT CHALK RIVER PLANT
speechtext: Until it can be cooled off it is impossible to decontaminate the reactor. Time has to elapse to allow the contamination to disappear, naturally. Until it can be decontaminated and the plant examined, it will be out of action. How long that will take, I could not tell you.

Mr. Speaker, I moved the adjournment of the debate yesterday so that I might finish this morning what I had to say on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I referred yesterday to the speech of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) who dealt in this house, on December 2 last, with the question of taxation rates and who also stated that the federal government did not take anything away from the provinces. I am of the same opinion.
The federal parliament has the exclusive power to raise funds by any method or system of taxation, either through direct or indirect taxes, whereas the provinces can levy direct taxes for provincial purposes only. These powers are conferred by sections 91 and 92 of the B.N.A. Act of 1867.
Has anyone replied to the speech made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet on that subject? Not at all. It is merely insinuated that the poor province of Quebec is being ill-treated.
The Ottawa government must discharge its obligations to the whole of Canada. In order to do so they must collect sufficient revenue through the methods of taxation at their disposal.
If, as was stated yesterday by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), the chamber of commerce approves the obstinate refusal by the premier of the province of Quebec to accept federal subsidies, it nevertheless recognizes the beneficial administration of the federal government. So true is this, in fact, that we can read the following in an article entitled "The Chamber of Commerce:	Facts and Trends," and dated March
19, 1952:
It is a fact that Canada's prestige in the community of nations is increasingly greater. Even the Americans recognize in this country one of the world's most progressive nations.
Immigration to Canada adds 150,000 new consumers each year to our population; a formidable figure. For industrialists and businessmen, these figures have far-reaching economic consequences.
In 1939, the gross value of Canadian production amounted to approximately 5 billion and a half; today, the gross value of this production amounts to 17 billion dollars.
Canada has been lucky enough to achieve a better balanced economy, which has made her more impervious to fluctuations on the markets of the world. In 10 years, iron and steel production has increased threefold; production of electric power has done even better and the volume of aluminum production has multiplied five times. In a single year, 1950, Canada manufactured more refrigerators than in 1938 and 1939 together.

The Address-Mr. Harkness
Eastern Canada draws a large part of its oil supply from the Alberta oil fields. Canadian oil fields compare favourably with the continent's most important fields. We have reserves for many centuries to come.
In a few years from now, i.e. in 1955, the works undertaken in Ungava will already have made possible the development of the amazing mineral deposits in that district. An output of 20 million tons a year is anticipated, once the St. Lawrence waterways project is completed.
Every year Canada receives foreign capital that helps her develop her natural resources. At the same time Canada is becoming more and more a creditor nation as far as the other countries of the world are concerned.
All these figures and statistics have but one aim: to give the assurance to the Canadian people that their country has boundless possibilities. We are a privileged people and we need but show initiative to provide for ourselves an enviable future.
If Canada has succeeded in gaining the attention of people of other countries, all the more reason for her own people to have confidence in her. We must not lose our optimism.
In view of that article and the few others I quoted last night, praising the Canadian government's administration, I believe we should all unite in a common effort as is suggested in the article entitled "Facts and Trends" published by the chamber of commerce.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some remarks in connection with the Currie report which was tabled in the house yesterday. I have had the report in my possession only for a very short time, and therefore I have not had an opportunity to read it and digest it thoroughly; but even on a first reading of it one is immediately struck by certain statements, some of which were pointed out to the house yesterday by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), and which are extremely disturbing.
It would help our understanding of the whole situation to go back and take up something in connection with the history back of this report. The first mention of it was in the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on April 21 of this year, to be found at page 1424 of Hansard of that date. I quote from the speech:
Mr. Speaker, following the discovery and investigation of grave irregularities in the engineer detachment at Petawawa camp, charges have been laid.
And so on. Then further down in the same remarks we find the following:
The irregularities first came to the attention of the department several months ago and arose out of the disposal of scrap under contracts made by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for the sale of thirty tons in 1950 and fifteen tons in 1951.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On what date was it first ascertained that there was any trouble?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In October, 1951.
According to this statement of the minister, the department knew, and he knew, that there was trouble there in October 1951, many months before the Petawawa irregularities were disclosed to the general public by the R.C.M.P. investigation. The question then immediately arises: if the department knew of these irregularities, why was nothing done about it? To begin with the minister says "following the discovery and investigation of grave irregularities in the engineering detachment"; in other words, the impression is given that the discovery of these irregularities was made only as a result of the R.C.M.P. investigation. By his own statement it will be seen that these irregularities were known for many months before that, back in October. As a matter of fact, if we refer to the report at page 4, and also appendix B, we see the same thing borne out. On page 4 Mr. Currie says:
It must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions.
And so forth. That is clear from appendix B. If you refer to appendix B you find, as a matter of fact, that the chief auditor reported on different dates twenty different types of irregularities. If you count them you will find that the number of these irregularities-I made a rapid count-are 159 altogether. These were not all at Petawawa; these were at different camps; but irregularities to the number of 159 had been reported in the years 1950, 1951 and 1952. In other words, the auditors were reporting irregularities at least as far back as 1950.
If we move from that to the reports of the defence expenditures committee of last year we find that reports quite evidently containing irregularities were made as far back as 1949. In the committee we had been talking about these auditors sent out by the auditor general of the department. Then at the close of the day I said, as reported at page 161 of the committee report:
Q. I have one more question. On page 16, it reads:
"At the close of an audit all matters requiring attention are discussed with the commanding officer and other officers concerned. A written report is forwarded to the assistant deputy minister covering each inspection, and he forwards it to the chief of staff concerned with his comments".
Now, I do not suppose you can answer these questions now, but you can bring them in next week.
The questions were:
When was the last inspection of this type made in Petawawa, and, secondly, when was the second last

inspection at Petawawa of this kind made, and thirdly, what was disclosed in regard to theft or material missing in each of these reports.
Well, the answers to these questions were brought in at the next meeting of the committee on May 8, and at page 172 the discussion is found. The point is that the only thing that was brought in was the dates, and after a long discussion any information as to what was concerned in those reports was denied, with various members on the government side of the house making specious arguments that it was not in the public interest to disclose, what was in those auditors' reports. It was quite evident that the only reason that the auditors' reports were not disclosed to the committee was that they contained reports of irregularities which the government at that time was anxious not to have made public. The dates on which these audits were made are rather significant. At page 173 a list of them is given. We find that audits of various units at Petawawa were made on June 18, 1951, June 5, 1951, May 12, 1950, another one on May 12, 1950, for another unit, May 6, 1950, May 23, 1949, May 6, 1950, May 1, 1949, and so on. Then, there were two more of them in 1949.
It is quite clear from this that these reports of irregularities had been coming in over a period of years to the Department of National Defence. Under the procedure they came to the assistant deputy minister or the deputy minister, and I am sure were referred to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). In spite of all these reports, apparently nothing was done to correct the situation, as appears in Mr. Currie's report, until after the matter became public as the result of the investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Now, if we refer back to the speech delivered by the Minister of National Defence on April 21 last we find he said this:
The investigation-
That is, the one at Petawawa.
-has disclosed no foundation for the reports alleging irregularities and deficiencies in the construction of buildings in the twenty-two major construction projects under way at Petawawa.
If one refers to the report, however, he finds at pages 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 of that report various irregularities, so far as construction is concerned. For instance, we find at page 8 that in certain cases-
-persons buying army material were asked not to make cheques in payment (in whole or in part) to the receiver general but to individual army personnel. The amounts thus paid did not reach the public treasury.
The Address-Mr. Harkness
Then a dam was built at Tucker creek at a cost estimated at some $3,000 or $4,000, and the report states:
Its utility is not clear to me, and it was, in any event, not authorized by army headquarters.
And so on. Therefore, in these cases we see irregularities, so far as construction matters are concerned. It is possible that none of these irregularities in construction was in the major projects which the minister mentioned specifically; but certainly it would be at least misleading to the house to say that no irregularities had been found in construction, and to attempt to say, as he did, that nothing irregular was found in connection with the twenty-two major construction projects.
As a matter of fact we find in four pages of this report various instances of irregularities, so far as construction is concerned. Then, if we turn to appendix B-and I am not going to deal with it in detail-we find that, so far as Petawawa is concerned, a considerable number of irregularities which occurred were regarding construction matters. They were in the nature of illegal work orders, and things of that kind.
Another matter to which the report refers is the lack of administrative and managerial ability, poor accounting, and things of that sort, so far as the army works people are concerned, and the finding that the same thing applies throughout. At page 17 of the report we find this statement in that connection:
The situation was complicated by still another factor. The Department of National Defence (including the army works services) was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime. Its establishment and administrative practices reflected more clearly the urgent needs and exigencies of war, when speed is everything and costs count not at all. The carry-forward of this war psychology . must be coupled with inadequate training and resultant ignorance on the part of personnel of their administrative duties and responsibilities.
That is the very thing about which those of us on this side of the house have complained on several occasions here, in the past. I am not going back to quote from Hansard, and to set out the particular instances of it. However, a. good deal of the difficulty in the Department of National Defence was because comparatively inexperienced men, so far as important administrative jobs were concerned, were in charge.
Once again, that is entirely the responsibility of the government. And it arose in this way, that following the war the government pursued the policy of dismissing practically all the men who had any considerable amount of experience before the war in what one might call general administrative work of the army. As a result they left in the

The policy followed was to retire .a considerable number of senior officers many years before the normal retirement age. This was not confined to officers, because many others including warrant officers, staff sergeants and the like, were retired years before their period of useful service was up. They were the very men who in the years before the war had been trained in accounting methods, administrative procedure and the like, required to run an army in peacetime. Ideas about economy and things of that nature just did not exist.

The Address-Mr. Harkness would seem to indicate a very strong necessity for a similar type of investigation and report on other branches of the service-as a matter of fact on the service as a whole.
The hon. member for Nanaimo last night pointed to and argued for the necessity of a commission to investigate defence matters generally. I think there is no doubt but that there is a strong necessity for something along that line.
This report contains a large number of important suggestions for improvement. There is one in particular to which I would just like to pay a small amount of attention. The suggestion is for the establishment of what is called a pilot plant. This suggestion is found on page 40 of the report:
Pilot Plant .
In view of the urgent need to apply immediate remedial measures, it is suggested that consideration be given to the setting-up of one of the army works companies as an example of the ideal to be attained. In choosing this special company, care should be taken to select one in a suitable area and with as nearly a perfect layout, equipment and facilities as is possible. The administrative arrangements, as well as the operational organization, should be most carefully set up to provide a model company. Such a company would be in the nature of a "pilot plant" to which officers and other ranks from other companies could be temporarily posted to obtain rapid and concentrated instruction as to how a works company should be organized and operated.
I think that is something that should be done not only so far as works companies are concerned but also throughout the services generally. For instance, it was one of the regular recognized procedures in the German army to have what were known as training battalions. It was by means of these training battalions that the German army was able to build itself up as rapidly as it did prior to the last war and to replace its losses as quickly as it did through recruits from training battalions. Canada what we say we intend to do. I believe that in due time the Liberal party will initiate national health insurance; and when they do, the people of Canada can look forward to a satisfactory health program.

Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose to explain why I shall not support the subamendment now before us, and also to deal with certain other matters now before the house. I think it is appropriate that an explanation should appear on the record as to why we propose to vote against the subamendment which, in itself, does not seem to raise any very serious questions, so far as the actual wording is concerned.
The subamendment reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
" (f) To bring before this house for adoption, a realistic financial and economic policy that will ensure the orderly development of Canada's resources, guarantee adequate markets at remunerative prices to producers, and provide to every Canadian his just share of the wealth our resources can be made to yield."
Those words, standing by themselves, might appear to be acceptable to most members in the house. I would point out, however, that in the very nature of any amendment or subamendment we must have regard to the interpretation placed upon those words by those who put them before the house for consideration.
There are many statements with which we would not disagree, in their general purport. For instance, there might be difficulty in understanding why anyone would vote against an amendment which expresses regret that the government has failed to introduce a plan for making every Canadian happy under every conceivable situation. But we would, of course, be bound to inquire into the kind of procedure that was contemplated to bring about happiness of that kind.
In this particular case, when we are attempting to decide whether that is the kind of financial and economic policy that we are prepared to support, we must find the interpretation of a realistic financial and economic policy from the explanations made by those who have put forward this subamendment. In the remarks that have been made in support of the subamendment we have been left in no doubt as to the kind of financial and economic policy that is referred to in the subamendment. That kind of policy, in the opinion of those who have put forward the subamendment for consideration, is a financial and economic policy in accord with their conception of social credit doctrine.

The Address-Mr. Drew
I use the words "their conception" advisedly, because I realize that there is a tremendous distinction between the social credit doctrines enunciated by Major Douglas and the social credit doctrines that emerged in this country from sources which have never been fully disclosed.
In so far as the economic policy of the social credit party is concerned I feel sure, from the statements that have been made in the house in support of the subamendment, that no question will be raised, and it would be appropriate to take their own statement of policy in that respect. Therefore I think it proper to read the statement of policy adopted by the Social Credit Association of Canada in 1944 which, I understand, has been followed since that time. It states:
The Social Credit Association of Canada reaffirms the three simple demands of Social Credit, namely:
(i)	To establish a national accounting system whereby we will know at stated intervals the net increase in our real wealth for which additional purchasing power must be created, free of debt and interest, and distributed to every man, woman and child in two ways-
(ii)	A dividend, paid at regular intervals, increasing as the national wealth increases; and
(iii)	A subsidy, or adjusted price on all wanted goods for sale by retailers;
And that the proportion of new purchasing power to be allotted to (ii) and (iii) be determined democratically by our representatives in parliament.
Mr. Speaker, if that is the idea of a realistic financial and economic policy which is to be interpreted by a resolution such as that now before us, then most certainly under no circumstances could I support this subamendment. Because what does not seem to be fully accepted by those who express their belief in this policy, with what I am sure is deep conviction, is the fact that the proposal they are making calls for an ironclad system of controls, without which no such system as this could possibly work. Nothing else would make a strange device of this kind possible.
The fact is that there has been very little evidence of the adoption of policies of this kind by a Social Credit government that has been in power for some years in the province of Alberta.

The reason the Social Credit government in Alberta has met with such continuing support as it has received is due to the fact that this doctrine never has been in effect in that province.
It is for these reasons that I certainly have no thought of supporting the subamendment. And may I say only this, with the utmost personal respect for some of the individuals who put these views before the house, that some of the statements made during this session in regard to financial policy for Canada read like statements out of "Alice in Wonderland". Far from being realistic, they are utterly unrealistic. They completely ignore any of the economic facts of life, and any government which attempted to run this country under a plan of that kind would rapidly encounter the most disastrous consequences.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with another subject that has come before us. It was raised in this house yesterday by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) in a manner which calls for comment on my part. I am referring to the statements that were made by the senior member for Queens (Mr. McLure) about Mr. Yousuf Karsh. In the statement of one of the most respected members of this house, and a man who has given inestimable service to the province from which he comes, he did in his anger, in relation to certain remarks that had been made, use a term which was taken out of an article appearing in a newspaper and which many hon. members of this house thought was only used in the context of the editorial. Hansard does disclose that the word was used in a way that might be open to misinterpretation.
I think that hon. members of this house, who know the intense pride of the people of that beautiful island province in their own island, are well aware of the way in which they naturally regard anything that appears to be a criticism of the province of which they are so intensely proud. I have known Mr. Yousuf Karsh for many years. I think it was unfortunate that he made the statements which he did about meals in Prince

When I have been there I have found that my great difficulty was to restrain my perpetual appetite for good food; and I do, in all seriousness, hope that I may have the opportunity some time of taking Mr. Yousuf Karsh to many places in Prince Edward Island where I have eaten food as good as I have eaten at any time or at any place I have been.
I think that perhaps from long acquaintance with Prince Edward Island, and from intimate association with the people of that island going back for many years, I can understand something of the anger that would oe aroused by the suggestion that their meals were not in keeping with the great traditions of that province. As a matter of fact, any such suggestion is denied by people who jo to Prince Edward Island as visitors. All one needs to do is to look at the list of visitors at any of the hotels in Prince Edward Island and he will find that people who can travel anywhere go there because of the lccommodation and good meals.
I might point out that one most respected nan who has lived in this country for many years, Field Marshal Alexander, while governor general, chose Prince Edward Island is a place to take his family when they were on their holidays. I think that in itself ihould remove any doubt about the quality of he meals of that island.
I do think that it was unfortunate that any ;uch comment was made and I can under-itand something of the resentment it would irouse.
Then, of course, there is something else. Those of us who know Prince Edward Island ilso recall what should be borne in mind n considering those words. I know that, in Yince Edward Island, most of us who have lot the privilege of having been born or irought up there are described as foreigners. That practice goes back to the early days vhen their pride in their own province, while t still remained out of confederation, made hem somewhat critical of those less fortunate vho lived in other parts of what is now Canada. That has carried forward and to nany the term is well known in Prince idward Island as one which is not used in the ame way that we use it. Nevertheless, I do now that the word as used and as reported in lansard is open to misinterpretation. It is or that reason that I am dealing with the latter today because I would not want to lave on the record an implication such as /as placed there yesterday in the remarks f one of the hon. members on the other side f the house. The word has been interpreted 
as applying to all those who were not born in Canada and who have chosen this country as their home.
Perhaps I should express resentment myself if that were to be the interpretation; because, if people are to be called foreigners under that formula, then, of course, my own wife would be described as a foreigner. I feel perfectly sure that no such interpretation was to be placed on the word but I do wish to make it perfectly clear that on all occasions when this subject has been under discussion, long before I had the privilege of entering the House of Commons, I have been emphatic in my statements that those who have chosen Canada as their homeland are Canadians- no matter where they were born or from what national stock they come. We welcome them to our country. We are welcoming many of them today. We wish to leave no thoughts in the mind of any one of them that there is in this country any distinction between one Canadian and another so long as that individual is a Canadian either by birth or by choice.
This country has built its strength by the blending together of people of different races and of different blood. The day is long past when we can regard the population of this country merely as a partnership between the two great races which joined hands many years ago to lay the foundation of this nation. In this country today we have large numbers of people whose blood stock stems back to many of the great nations of Europe and of other parts of the world.
I wish to make quite clear that when I refer to my own position in this house I am stating the position of our party, repeated and emphasized many times, that there are no foreigners in Canada except those who are simply visiting Canada from some foreign land, and that every person who has chosen Canada as his or her home is a Canadian and we regard them as good Canadians unless their conduct in any way challenges that position. May I say that Mr. Yousuf Karsh is a distinguished Canadian and has been a distinguished Canadian for many years. He is a Canadian who has brought honour to this country by great attainment in what is today one of the most important arts. Not only is he a great Canadian but he has resisted many inducements, which must have been very appealing, to go elsewhere.
Having known him personally for many years, I am aware that from many of the great cities of the United States offers have come to him which from a financial viewpoint were most attractive. I know that the reason he has stayed here is that he cherishes his Canadian citizenship, and for that very reason

he has demonstrated that he is a Canadian citizen who is prepared to maintain that citizenship by choice and by preference. Again may I say that this is something that need not have been discussed at this length were it not for the manner in which it was introduced into the house yesterday afternoon. I very much regret the fact that the hon. member for Ottawa West sought to imply that a comment by the senior member for Queens (Mr. McLure) that had been made in the context to which I have referred was an interpretation of the attitude of the Conservative party.
At the same time he made a political speech about the record of the Liberal party which was strangely out of place for an hon. member who has sat in this house during this session and has applauded the continuing appeals to prejudice which have been made by different members since the session began. I would also point out that it is hardly appropriate for the hon. member for Ottawa West to speak about this subject in terms of such self-righteousness at the very time that the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Kickham) was interjecting into the discussion these words: "If the hon. member made such a statement in Armenia he would be kicked out of the country".
I merely point out that the statement that was being referred to was the same statement by Mr. Karsh. Let us not for one moment pretend that careless comments or words which were not intended in the manner in which they appear in the context are the fault of any single member of the house. I certainly would be the last to pretend that there are not many words I have spoken that could be taken out of their context and meaning and so interpreted. I suspect that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would not suggest that there were not words of his that from time to time might have been open to similar misinterpretation. I suspect that there is hardly a single member of the house who can say in complete sincerity, as he looks back over the many things that have been said, that there is nothing that could be taken out of its general context and interpreted in a manner which was never intended.
Therefore I leave this subject simply with the expressed hope that a statement provoked by a criticism of something that is associated with a proud province, a province which has great justification for its pride, will not in any way be taken as interpreting either the general sentiments of the member who expressed his dislike of the criticism in the first place or of any of the members of the party to which he belongs. I wish to deal now, Mr. Speaker, with certain aspects of the Currie report, and the implications of that report in relation to the wider problems of national defence. In considering the importance of any aspect of this problem, it is essential that we bear in mind that the whole question is one which is primarily connected with national survival. We are not discussing the ordinary administration of any department. We are discussing the effectiveness of that department upon whose activities our contribution to the common defences of freedom is going to depend in very large measure. Therefore, we must examine any information we receive in regard to the effectiveness of that department with due consideration as to its possible bearing upon the whole question of defence, an extremely important question in relation to whether the enormous sums being spent on defence are being spent in the most efficient manner.
Before I proceed to deal with that part of the discussion, I wish to return to certain questions and answers which are recorded in Hansard of this session. First, I wish to read from Hansard of December 1, 1952, page 203. Before the orders of the day, I asked the following question:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Can he inform us when he will receive the report which we were assured was being prepared some time ago by Mr. Currie with respect to the administration of the Department of National Defence so far as it affects Petawawa camp?
The answer of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was as follows:
I have not been in touch with Mr. Currie myself for some time but I am informed by the deputy minister that he has been in touch with members of Mr. Currie's staff, and that it is expected that the report will be available within the next week or two. It has not been made yet.
Then I asked a supplementary question as follows:
As a supplementary question, may I ask whether the government has received an interim report?

The Address-Mr. Drew The Minister of National Defence replied, no.
Then on- December 4, as recorded in Hansard at page 321, there are the following questions and answers:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day, in view of the fact that it has been announced that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) will be leaving tomorrow, I wish to direct a question to him. I ask whether, since Mr. Currie's appointment was announced on April 21, 1952, he has received any positive recommendations from Mr. Currie in regard to the subject matter of his inquiry, in writing or orally, and if so is the minister prepared to convey to the house some information as to the nature of the recommendations which have been made.
To this the Minister of National Defence replied:
Mr. Speaker, since Mr. Currie's appointment I have seen him about this matter on one occasion only. That was when he was in national defence headquarters carrying on his inquiry. I asked him to see me and he did. I then asked him if he was getting all the information that he wanted and he said he was. I told him that if at any time he wanted further powers or more information such would be made available to him.
I have had no other communication of whatever kind with him.
Then I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask a supplementary question. In view of the fact that the minister read to us a letter from Mr. Currie, assuring us at the time of his appointment that he would proceed with the utmost speed to make inquiry into this matter and communicate his views to the minister, may I ask if the minister has pointed that out to him and has he not indicated that it is very desirable that we have the report at the earliest possible date.
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I have not interfered with Mr. Currie's investigation in any way whatever. He knows as well as the Leader of the Opposition that it is desirable that a report should be made at the earliest possible date.
I then said:
Mr. Speaker, I ask one further supplementary question. To the knowledge of the minister, has Mr. Currie seen the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in regard to this matter within recent weeks?
The minister answered:
I have no information bearing on that at all. Had Mr. Currie seen the Prime Minister I am sure the Prime Minister would have spoken to me about it. Since he has not done so I assume that Mr. Currie has not seen him.
Then I said:
There seems a strange lack of interest in such an important matter.
May I just repeat the words in this question and answer. I asked, and I am quoting:
. . . whether, since Mr. Currie's appointment was announced on April 21, 1952, he has received any positive recommendations from Mr. Currie in regard to the subject matter of his inquiry, in writing or
TMr. Drew.]
orally, and if so is the minister prepared to convey to the house some information as to the nature of the recommendations which have been made.
To that the reply was that there was no information available. Then on December 8, as recorded at page 415 of Hansard, I said:
I wish to direct a question to the Acting Minister of National Defence. Is he in a position yet to inform us definitely when we may receive a copy of the report by Mr. Currie which was promised us last spring?
The reply was:
No, Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to say because I have not received the report yet myself.
I then said as follows:
Will the acting minister take steps to find out from Mr. Currie when the report will be available?
The reply was:
From the remarks which the minister made in the house a few days ago I understood that Mr. Currie had indicated that the report would be forthcoming within a week or ten days. I presume that estimate was made with knowledge of what was possible on his part. I do not mind making inquiry if it is desired.
I then said:
I would point out that the minister made a general statement with regard to that before he made the statement in the house that he had not been in touch with Mr. Currie. It is for that reason I ask the direct question: Will the acting minister find out from Mr. Currie when the report will be ready?
Then on December 12, in the absence of the minister and the acting minister, I directed a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence as follows:
In the absence of the Minister of National Defence as well as the Acting Minister of National Defence, I should like to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence. Can he assure us that the report by Mr. George S. Currie will be presented to this house before we rise for the Christmas recess?
The parliamentary assistant replied as follows:
I have no information on that matter, Mr. Speaker. I shall take it as notice of a question.
I then said:
In view of the assurances given last spring, may I ask that steps be taken towards ascertaining when this report will be ready?
The parliamentary assistant replied:
As I recall, Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of National Defence left this question was asked, and he replied that the report would be given in the course of the next few days.
I then said:
Mr. Speaker, I am directing my remarks to you in the form of a question. Last spring, on April 21, assurance was given to this house that a report was to be presented at the earliest possible date. This house acted upon that statement. In answer to several requests we have been given no information, and I suggest that the department is in contempt of this house in the course it is following.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that those questions and answers are extremely important and that the implications of them go far beyond any question of the accuracy or otherwise of statements that have been made or of the nature of the report now before us. We had the positive statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), or certainly a clear impression was conveyed, that neither in writing nor orally had he received any positive suggestions from Mr. Currie. Mr. Speaker, the whole effect of the answers given to the questions that I have read is that the minister, the acting minister and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence knew nothing about this report and that they were simply awaiting the natural processes of the original instructions which had been given. In the light of that impression and of the statements which I have read, I find it difficult indeed to see how anything but the most serious impression can be left by the words of Mr. Currie in presenting this report to the Minister of National Defence. I would point out that it is dated November 26. It is a report by a man who has been recognized on both sides of this house as one of great competence, integrity and business experience. I think we still require some explanation as to what happened between November 26 and December 8. I should particularly like to point out these words in the letter from Mr. Currie to the minister which began the report. On the very first page I find these words addressed to the minister:
It should be noted that interim suggestions made bv me during my investigations have already been seized on and important reforms are already being carried out.
Mr. Speaker, is it possible for any hon. member of this house to be in any doubt that those suggestions were made to the Minister of National Defence? Is it possible for any hon. member of this house to doubt that in any event those suggestions were brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence? Let it be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Currie has said "important reforms are already being carried out". I hope that no one is going to suggest that important reforms have been carried out without the minister's knowing anything about them. I must confess that it would almost seem that this might have been a happy accident, but surely that cannot be the case. Surely any inefficiency that existed cannot have reached the point that reforms in the Department of National Defence have been carried out without the minister's knowing about them or knowing the basis upon which those reforms have been introduced. I leave the matter there, but I ask every
The Address-Mr. Drew hon. member of this house to go back over those questions and answers, to read those words of Mr. Currie, and to consider in all earnestness whether any hon. member of this house in future has any right to accept any assurance of the present Minister of National Defence with regard to any aspect of the administration of his department.

I said that I accepted your ruling and acted accordingly, and I did. I am proceeding to deal with the report and I assure you that any attempts that may be made to hedge this report about with any technical restrictions will not impress the public of Canada, in view of the disclosures that are in it.
I have pointed out that on page 1 of this report Mr. Currie has pointed out in clear and implicit words that he made recommendations by way of interim suggestions, and that some of these had been acted upon. Then, on page 3, I come to the disclosure of what happened at Petawawa, and in reading these words I wish to deal with the very obvious attempt that has been made, and what would appear to be part of a concerted plan, to lay the blame for what has happened upon members of the army.
Under our parliamentary system of responsible government, it is the goverment that is responsible if anything has gone wrong. It is not only the Department of National Defence that is responsible; it is the government, under our system of joint responsibility, and that seems to be completely disregarded by this government in so many instances.
I wish to point out that at page 3 Of the report Mr. Currie refers to the Department of National Defence. He is not referring to the army, to the brass hats, as we heard from some of the hon. members this morning on the other side. I quote his words which appear at page 3:
... it is an unhappy circumstance that the beginning of this investigation lies not inside the Department of National Defence and its full com-

plement of regulations and supervising personnel, but with the receipt -of an anonymous letter couched in the following terms:
"The Commissioner, Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,
There is reason to believe that an illegal transaction of army goods has taken place between army personnel of No. 3 works coy., R.C.E., and . . . company within the past few days.
This transaction involves the selling of several railway carloads of cook stoves and heaters without proper army authority."
Then the letter goes on to suggest places where this may be followed up. On the page following we find again that it is not the army, it is not the general staff, it is not the engineering services that are mentioned; it is the Department of National Defence. I quote the words of Mr. Currie:	"
It must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions.
In the words of Mr. Currie, the auditor of the Department of National Defence had reported to the Department of National Defence unsatisfactory conditions, and, according to Mr. Currie, had performed his functions conscientiously.
After having described various things that had happened and losses that had taken place Mr. Currie said at the bottom of page 9 of the report:
How many more there may have been will never be known.
And then he went on, on page 11, after having recounted some of the detail:
My view would be, however, that the generally lax administrative situation would give rise to waste and inefficiency far more costly in loss than that covered by actual dishonesty.
Then on page 15 of the report we come to the statement which is perhaps the most important one in the whole report. When we recognize the fact that this department is spending approximately half of all the moneys collected by taxes from the people of Canada at this time, these words should be read with that in mind:
If there is excuse for inefficient accounting, there is none for the failure of security which is, after all, a prime military consideration. I take a serious view of this break-down. If it is easy to pilfer military stores, then, by the same token, it is easy to sabotage military equipment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first glimmer of hope that discussion in this

parliament is actually producing results. We
have at least accomplished one reform this afternoon in this respect.
Now, the report that we have before us does not by any manner of means refer to only the army or to the army works services. May I just read these words from page 17 to indicate how directly this report is related to the very point, to the Department of National Defence, and I quote:
The Department of National Defence (including the army works services) was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime.
That is the end of the quotation and the author was dealing with the Department of National Defence, pointing out that steps had not yet been taken to bring the whole organization into line with the requirements of peace. It is the Department of National Defence. And, Mr. Speaker, I hope that no attempt will be made to find scapegoats either in the general staff or in the ranks of the army for a department which must, under our responsible system, accept full responsibility for what has happened.
This is not by any means the first time that this subject has been before the house. The subject has been under discussion over and over again and the need for a full examination of the whole military set-up, and its place in relation to the Department of National Defence, has been emphasized again and again for the last three years. I shall quote from words that I addressed to this house on November 3, 1949. I am quoting from page 1405 of Hansard for that date:
This is not a new subject. Over and over again in the past the same arguments have been made, and the advances that have taken place throughout the years have been as a result of the appointment of committees of some kind which could inquire into the real requirements of our defence forces, and their efficient organization for the tasks they might be called upon to undertake. The modern army system in Great Britain, which we in Canada have followed to a considerable extent, came about as a result of the findings of the famous Esher committee of 1904. Demands have been made since the time of the South African war for an inquiry into the organization of the forces, the suitability of training, and their ability to undertake any tasks they might be called upon to perform in the future. It was not until that committee was appointed that the errors that had been so apparent in the South African war were overcome, and an effective reorganization took place under the modern general staff system. Other famous and important inquiries followed at different times. After the first world war General Otter made his famous findings known as the Otter report. In it was laid down the appropriate organization of the land defence forces of Canada, and the way in which they should be trained for the tasks they might be called upon to undertake.
It was not for some years that effective steps were taken to bring about the necessary reorganization, and in the meantime much had happened.

The Address-Mr. Drew
In 1933 and 1934 extensive inquiries were conducted by the conference of defence associations, a body which embraced both permanent and non-permanent officers of the defence services of Canada. It was as a result of their recommendations that the reorganization took place which made it possible for Canada to mobilize its forces effectively at the outbreak of the last war.
Another war has passed. Four years have elapsed since it ended. The evidence is now clear on all sides that it is essential that there be an examination of the over-all plan of national defence, the suitability of the organization of our forces for that plan, the effectiveness of the training that is undertaken, and the proper expenditure of the money devoted to this purpose. There is no occasion to go into the past. We are confronted today with the necessity of spending enormous sums of money, approximately $400 million. Only a few days ago it was indicated to us that a bill would be presented for the unification of the defence forces of Canada. Unification undoubtedly is highly desirable, but unification will not be very effective unless the forces which are unified have themselves been placed in proper relationship to other forces, having regard to what is conceived to be Canada's particular place in the general over-all picture today.
It is only by the assessment of our requirements that we can know whether our money is being properly spent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that I was there referring to $400 million which we then regarded as an enormous sum. Now it is more than $2 billion, and by just that extent the importance of knowing where the money is going has increased.
I want to read these words from the reply of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) which indicate, as clearly as words can indicate, what the attitude has been at any time we have sought to emphasize the need for an inquiry of this nature. I read from Hansard of November 3, 1949, page 1415, these words by the Minister of National Defence:
With regard to organization, X believe X can say without fear of successful contradiction that in the work of unification, co-ordination and the streamlining of our forces, navy, army and air forces, the Department of National Defence of- Canada has made more progress than any other country in the world.
That, Mr. Speaker, has been the whole attitude of the department when any suggestion has been made that there could be improvements. The answer has been: No, we are better than anybody else in the world- and no recommendations were given serious consideration.
We have before us now, Mr. Speaker, recommendations which cannot possibly be disregarded. That pompous facade, which has been presented over and over by this government, has been torn apart and torn apart permanently by this present report.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
No more can these arrogant assurances that the Department of National
Defence is above any suggestion of improvement possibly have the slightest sound of reality, in view of the disclosures of this report. It is the Department of National Defence that is condemned by this report; and the Department of National Defence must accept responsibility. It is the Department of National Defence that is challenged by every report now before us.
We want no scapegoats for the minister and those within his department who should be called upon by this department to accept the full responsibility. May I add something more. It is not only the responsibility of the department, it is the responsibility of the whole government until it acts in some way to deal effectively with this situation. The attitude of the members of the government in this respect was disclosed in a very remarkable way by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on December 8. I would point out that it is very significant that it was December 8, because we are informed that was the day this report was delivered. On that day the Secretary of State for External Affairs interpolated into his speech on foreign affairs the following words, as found at page 418 of Hansard:
By way of interpolation, and to dispel any remaining suspicion which may linger in his mind in regard to the relationship of myself and my department to that matter, I would merely say at this time-to clear the matter up, and I hope that it will as far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned-that neither I nor my department made any representations, oral or written, formal or informal, to the Department of National Defence about Brigadier Connelly and the Koje incident at any time. Neither I nor my department have had anything whatever to do with his retirement. That, Mr. Speaker, is by way of an aside which I consider in the circumstances to be necessary, as I did not have the privilege of attending the session of the house when this matter came up.
Let me emphasize these words: "Neither I nor my department have had anything whatever to do with his retirement." Under our system of collective responsibility, Mr. Speaker, every member of the government is responsible for every act of the government. As a member of the government the Secretary of State for External Affairs is responsible for what has happened to Brigadier Connelly. Did I hear a member of the government say "no"?

It certainly has been reemphasized so far as I am concerned and I am sure-

It certainly does reinforce confidence in Mr. Currie because he has dealt frankly with the problem before him and has placed the responsibility squarely on the shoulders of the Department of National Defence and in turn the government. This report deals only with the part of the responsibility of the Department of National Defence with which Mr. Currie was directed to deal. Already the suggestion has been made that further inquiries are necessary. I should think that the very wording of the report and its findings make it clear that further inquiries are necessary at the very earliest date. Moreover, it is clear that further independent inquiries, of the same kind as those which took place and which have led to this very important report, are necessary.
Therefore I make the suggestion to the government in all earnestness, and with the proof before them of the effectiveness of the procedure, that they reappoint Mr. Currie to conduct an inquiry into every aspect of the organization and accounting methods of the Department of National Defence. Here we have a report dealing with one part of the activities of the department. Here we have a report that I feel sure will stand the


test of challenge. Here we have a report that has expressed impartial findings. If the government wishes to deal effectively with the problem now before us, I urge them to reappoint Mr. Currie without delay, to give him the widest authority and to permit him to inquire into every aspect of the organization, accounting methods and other related duties of the Department of National Defence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one thing that has alarmed me in listening to this debate so far has been the attitude taken by some members on the government side of the house who, through their interjections, have indicated that the main people to be condemned as a result of the report which was tabled yesterday are the members of the general staff. We have a democratic government in Canada, and this year we are spending some $2,100 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money to build up the armed forces of the country in order to protect us. If the interjections are indications of the attitude of the government toward their general staff, who are responsible for the building of this security, then I am afraid we are not getting very much for our money. It seems to me if we are to have security there must be co-operation and confidence between the government and the general staff, not bickering, as would appear from the interjections that have been made so far in this debate.
I should like to deal with the manner in which the report was tabled. When tabling the report yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) also tabled a letter from General Simonds. The government appointed Mr. Currie to make an investigation into certain things which were taking place in our armed forces. A report was made by Mr. Currie and was presented to the government, but instead of presenting the report to parliament by itself as it stood a letter from General Simonds, the head of the army, was tabled with it. I should like an explanation from the Prime Minister as to why that procedure was followed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is exactly what I feared. The government apparently was more interested in protecting the people whom they were investigating than in protecting the money of the people of this country.
The Prime Minister indicated that he hoped we would not take pieces of this report out of their context, and use them. I was surprised that the Prime Minister should be the first to do that. As a matter of fact, he used one sentence, and this is the sentence:
It does not fit the facts to indict or to smear the whole army works services personnel because of the sins of a handful of crooks.
Now, let me read what went before that to see whether it was taken in its context. Before that, Mr. Currie said:
The contents of this chapter are chiefly based upon my studies there-
That is at Petawawa.
-because of the existence there of a combination of factors; lax control, poor discipline and the presence of dishonest personnel. The combination proved disastrous.
It is mentioned in this context chiefly for the purpose of praising the personnel at other depots for not walking through the door which a fundamentally loose situation had opened before them.
In other words, the Department of National Defence has left doors open, and the commissioner commends the armed forces for not doing more pilfering. Time and again in the report it is indicated that it is the Department of National Defence that is responsible for this situation. It is indicated that the auditor general of the Department of National Defence made reports to the government pointing out irregularities that were taking place, yet no action was taken as a result of those reports. Time and again that took place. What possible excuse can the government have when they were notified that these irregularities were taking place and yet failed to take any action to prevent them?
The Address-Mr. Wright
I am sure that if any hon. member of this house were a member of a town council or a city council and he dismissed the police force and took no adequate measures to protect the people in his community, he would be severely criticized. Yet here we find that the Department of National Defence, after repeated notices, has failed to take the necessary measures to protect the people of this country from pilfering and irregularities. The ministry and the individual members of the government have tried repeatedly in this house to indicate that this was just petty pilfering; that it did not amount to very much. Well, that is not what Mr. Currie says in his report. He has indicated that it is a serious matter. It is a very serious matter for instance when a dam is built in a certain creek at a cost estimated from $3,000 to $4,000, and Mr. Currie says:
Its utility is not clear to me, and it was, in any event, not authorized by army headquarters.
Up in that area that dam is known by a certain name, and certain officers go up there to fish in. the pool which just happened to be created.

The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver), in a speech delivered earlier this session, tried to indicate to the house that this did not amount to very much and that adequate measures were being taken to correct anything that might have been wrong. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) indicated that it was quite possible there was something seriously wrong at Penhold in Alberta with regard to the construction of housing. What indication has the government given that they have taken any notice of his speech? What investigations are they carrying out to see that this is not general across the country and not just in the particular department that has been investigated?
I want to say this, that this government have deliberately, through their policies, encouraged this sort of thing. Last year in

The Address-Mr. Wright this house we voted approximately $2,100 million for defence purposes, while the year before we voted $1,725 million, when the government knew that there were not the facilities in this country to produce the goods and services that amount of money represented. Here is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said in this house on April 8, 1952, as recorded at page 1247 of Hansard:
Last year we planned, and parliament authorized, defence expenditures in the total amount of $1,725 million. Actually we have spent about $1,441 million, or a shortfall of $284 million. How could this come about? Let me give an example. We had planned and expected to spend about $210 million on major defence construction projects; but because of difficulties of design and construction, and shortages of labour and materials, we have found it possible to spend only about $165 million on these projects before the end of the year. The acquisition of machine tools and of military equipment and its components in the United States poses exceptionally difficult problems of estimation as to final cost, delivery dates and dates of payment. In the year just ended the story has been one of unavoidable delays and postponements.
In other words, we voted the money and this government should have known, through its economic experts, how much military equipment this country could produce in any given year to take up that amount of money. When you vote a department more money than they could possibly spend, more money than the facilities of this country are capable of producing goods to take up, then it seems to me you are asking for trouble. You are giving people money in huge amounts when there are no physical goods upon which they can spend it. As a result, you get the sort of spending that is indicated in the Currie report. Surely, if this government wants to use the people's money in an economic way to create the security and the armed forces that are necessary for this country, they should use some reasonable methods of control.
We are not getting the security we should have in this country. If someone can walk into a camp like Petawawa and walk off with a railroad siding or walk off with 18 carloads of cement, there could be sabotage in such a camp. There is no system of checks set up by our Department of National Defence. This makes it possible for people to walk into camps across this country and walk away with goods to the extent that has been indicated.

does not the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) ask the Minister of National Defence some of these questions that he is asking me? He is the man who must give to this House of Commons answers to these questions, not the hon. member for Kindersley. The minister has consistently made little of these things; he has told this house that there is nothing much the matter, just a little bit of pilfering which may take place around any army camp. That is not what this report indicates. This report indicates on the part of the Department of National Defence neglect to use the proper supervisory methods that are necessary when any department is spending the sums of money that this department is spending. When this government imposes on the people of this country taxes for the purpose of procuring security for the country, they have a right to see that that money is spent in a manner which will obtain that security and to see that it is not frittered away as is indicated in this report.
I will be interested to hear what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has to say with regard to this matter, and I will be interested to hear what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has to say. It seems passing strange that, after two days of debate, no member of the government has yet seen fit to take part in this debate. It seems to me that they are a long time in reaching some decision with regard to the matter. This is not something new. This report is something that was asked for by the government. Mr. Currie was appointed to make this report. That fact indicates that the government knew that certain things were taking place or they would not have called on Mr. Currie to make this report. Yet now, when the report is tabled here, it seems to come as so much of a surprise to the government that nobody seems to be able to rise and say anything about it.

The point is this, Mr. Speaker. A serious condition has existed for a considerable length of time but as yet we have had from the government no indication as to what remedies they are going to apply. The sooner we get that indication from the government the better satisfied will be the people of Canada, because the people of Canada have indicated their willingness to see that sufficient money is made available for the security of this country but they want one thing. They want that money spent in a way that will bring security, not in a way that leaves the back door open in every camp in this country so that someone can walk in and take what he likes. That is the situation that is indicated at Petawawa in this report, where the front door was locked but the back door was open.
I am not going to deal with the matter of the two reports; it can be dealt with later. From this report it is perfectly evident that the tendency on the part of the government has been to blame the fellow down below. This report shifts the whole emphasis of responsibility-the unabridged report, as it has been called by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson), shifted it even more-to the higher echelons. I hope this government will not try to absolve itself by blaming either the top brass or the small man in the army, because the matter goes farther than that. The pilfering and the misspending that took place were the result of lack of proper supervision, and that proper supervision could be given only by the Department of National Defence. It is the Department of National Defence which must answer to parliament and to the people of Canada for the disclosures that are made in this report.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak again in this debate, but the report tabled in this house yesterday made it necessary. At the outset I want to commend Mr. Currie on the fearless and complete report that he apparently drew up. I am going to qualify that statement just slightly because I am not quite satisfied that the report that was tabled in the house is the same as the original report given out by Mr. Currie. I was amazed to find that there is apparently another report in circulation somewhere. How our friends of the C.C.F. got hold of it, I do not know; and I imagine there are many other members in the house who are more interested in that fact than I am.
From some of the conversations I have heard, I would gather that many of the members of this house seem to think it a crime that the C.C.F. were able to get hold of the original copy of this report. I do not
The Address-Mr. Thomas think the crime is in their getting hold of it or in the fact that it did get loose. I think the crime in the whole matter, Mr. Speaker, is that the original report was not given to this house in the first place.
From Mr. Currie's report it is quite apparent that the original complaint came not from the Department of National Defence but from an anonymous letter which was quoted earlier by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew); and as it appears in this report, there is no date on it nor is there any indication as to when that letter was received by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I should like to know-as, I am sure, would other hon. members of the house-just when that letter was placed in the hands of the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. That information might be quite interesting, because we should like to know just how long it was prior to this request for an investigation that this letter was received.
From the report it is quite apparent that the accounting system, as laid down by the government, is good but that the execution and enforcement of it is poor. Last year when the committee sat we were quite well informed as to the organization and the accounting system, and I must say that I was greatly impressed. But during the committee sittings last year we were unable to dig into the enforcement angle of the regulations. I had hoped at that time that we should be able to do so, and I still hope that we shall be able to dig in and get much more information when the committee is set up this session.
I was quite amazed, as apparently was the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), that the taking of 18,000 bags of cement is termed "petty pilfering". I can agree with the hon. member for Melfort when he says that that amount represents 18 box cars full. I telephoned the Canadian National Railways freight department today and found out that it would take just exactly that number of box cars to hold that many bags of cement. As the report indicates, the cement was only a test case. There were over 5,000 other items which could have been delved into, but which he thought would not be necessary. It would be interesting to know just how far things have gone as far as these other 5,000 items are concerned.
As far as the petty pilfering of a complete C.P.R. spur line is concerned, I just wonder how many men it would take to raise those tracks, and then when fear of detection came along they lifted the C.N.R. track to replace the C.P.R. or, I wonder, as one gentleman said, is that the job that the horses did. While we are on the subject of horses, I would

The Address-Mr. Thomas suggest that the government might dig into some of the other departments of government and find out whether any of these horses are married and are drawing family allowances, or are they on old age pension.
