You would wonder sometimes, would you not?
Apparently the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) wants the sole responsibility to lie in the hands of the lower departments of the army. It is quite apparent from this report that the blame cannot be placed there. As reported on page 3, a part of which was quoted by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) today, the fault lies entirely within the Department of National Defence, or partially so. Originally, the fault may have been in the army, because undoubtedly that is where the pilfering came from. But the continuation of that pilfering is directly the responsibility of the Department of National Defence and nobody else. I shall repeat what the Leader of the Opposition read, because I think it could bear repeating. This is what appears on page 4 of the report:
... it must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from appendix B which summarizes his findings over a period of years. The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, after a second auditor's report it was the responsibility of the deputy minister of national defence to insist on some sort of investigation. It is quite true that frequently you find incompetency, laxity, and sometimes dishonesty among army personnel and among the officers; but the department must have known that this was going on, because the auditor of the Department of National Defence had brought it to the attention of the deputy minister on many occasions. Therefore the responsibility rests entirely on the shoulders of that department and upon the government and on no one else.
I noticed one thing on looking into this report, and possibly it is outside the realm of investigation. I should like to know a little bit more about the construction programs that are going on, the awarding of contracts, and I should also like to know whether mention of those contracts, and so on, were in the original copy, as the hon. member says, the unabridged copy, of this report.
	_
Mr. Currie says that these things went on chiefly in Petawawa. Probably they were not carried on to such a great extent in the other centres throughout Canada, but there is no doubt in my mind that the same thing is going on in many places, although perhaps on a smaller scale.
As I travel around through various parts of the country I hear men, army personnel, officers, complain and say: "For goodness' sake, is there not something we can do to get rid of this waste, not only of material but of time?" As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, at one army centre-and this is directly hearsay; I am not going to vouch for the authenticity of it-I was talking to one of the employees and he was telling of a truckload of cedar shingles that disappeared. Apparently the truck driver drove out of the camp with these shingles, and sometime later the truck came back empty. When he was asked by one of the other employees where the shingles had gone he replied-to use his own words-"None of your damn business."
The fact that the other camps Eire not as badly off as Petawawa shows that army personnel and the civilians working for the Department of National Defence in those various centres are fundamentally honest. But it is no credit whatsoever to the government, or to government policy, that every other camp in this country is not in the same condition as Petawawa. As a matter of fact, I would say that instead of saying, as a result of government policy these camps are not so bad, we should say: in spite of government policy these men were able to remain honest and to look after their jobs in a conscientious sort of way.
As I said before, I do not think there is any doubt in the world that this demonstrates an absolute failure of the government,, not of the army, to enforce regulations. If it were a matter of poor regulations or a poor set-up, there might be some excuse for it, because they had not found the right way of doing it. But in view of the fact that Mr. Currie says the regulations are adequate if they are enforced, it leads me to say that it is not a matter of policy but one of enforcement, and the government is at fault. Let the government either correct these faults or face the consequences.
Just to go one little bit further, this involves more than the Department of National Defence, because on page 19 of this report Mr. Currie says:
In all cases, the treasury officer, who is appointed by the Department of Finance to work within the Department of National Defence, must certify that the necessary money is available and that the expenditure is in fact in accordance with the purpose for which the funds were voted.

In other words, not only the Department of National Defence but also the Department of Finance is equally at fault. Probably the Department of Defence Production, because they have a finger in it, may also be at fault. In all probability they are involved as well as the armed forces. I would be one of the first to say that it is only a small portion of the armed forces, only a small group, that is at fault. We have three distinct departments of government involved, and unless some drastic step is taken I am afraid that the government is going to find itself in a pretty unenviable position, and it is a position of its own making, and I cannot say that I feel too sorry for it.

Mr. Speaker, in the past few days much has been said in the newspapers and over the radio about the recent happenings at Louise-ville which have brought about the proclamation of the Riot Act. To understand the situation fully, it must be recalled that the strike at Louiseville, which has been going on for more than nine months, was called as a result of a labour dispute between the national syndicate of textile workers at Louiseville and the Associated Textiles of Canada Limited. The said strike constitutes a record in the history of labour relations in Canada.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that what has happened at Louiseville since the beginning of that strike will not bring unfavourable publicity to the town of Louiseville and will not be detrimental to its economic welfare nor to its excellent reputation.
Louiseville is a small industrial centre located between Montreal and Three Rivers. Its inhabitants are and have always been naturally peaceful in their behaviour. All classes of society live in perfect harmony and everybody has at heart the progress and the development of the town. The workers also enjoy an enviable reputation.
I take this opportunity to tell the working classes and the whole population that I sympathize with them. These people are now going through a very painful experience. Business is on the decline and I do hope that a solution will be found before it is too late.
I also take this opportunity to offer my congratulations to the whole population of Louiseville who, since the beginning of the strike that threatens to paralyse the whole economic structure of this locality, have displayed an extraordinary degree of courage and patience.
The Address-Mr. J. Langlois
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred yesterday to what happened at Louiseville. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not share the opinions expressed by the hon. member, who asked the Minister of Labour to launch an investigation into what has been going on at Louiseville for nearly a year. The strike at Louiseville is, indeed, a labour dispute over which the province has exclusive jurisdiction and no one, as far as I know, has challenged this jurisdiction. The parties themselves have never complained about it. Since the beginning, I have followed every phase of the dispute very closely and I would have intervened myself long ago, had I deemed it advisable to do so. Knowing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) as I do, I am convinced that had this question been under federal jurisdiction, it would have been possible to arrive at a solution satisfactory to both management and workers.
Now, the Riot Act has been read. I am still convinced that this business is no concern of the Department of Labour. The Riot Act is a part of the Criminal Code which, under the constitution, is administered by the provinces. And so federal intervention in this connection, if only for purposes of inquiry, would be considered as a violation of provincial rights in the field of labour relations.
Even in so far as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is concerned, I hold that the federal Department of Labour can -only intervene at the request of the provincial department and after an agreement has been concluded between the provincial and federal governments.
Mr. Speaker, my remarks today are directed especially to the Minister of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission. I wish to bring to their attention the difficulties the Louiseville strikers find themselves in from the point of view of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Under section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, all strikers are deprived of their right to unemployment benefits as long as work stoppage lasts. Since, in this case, such stoppage has lasted for more than nine months, these workers have not been able to pay any unemployment insurance contributions since March 10 last, the date on which the strike was declared. I suggest that the Louiseville strikers no longer comply with the statutory conditions required by section 28 of the Unemployment Insurance Act and that they cannot claim the right to draw unemployment insurance benefits. If, Mr. Speaker, this

The Address-Mr. P. E. Cote strike should be settled tomorrow, and if, after a few days, the employer should be forced, due to highly important considerations, to lay off some of his employees for lack of work, there is no doubt that all these unemployed workers would be deprived of their right to benefits, on account of their having failed to pay the contributions required within the period of time laid down by section 28.
I therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Labour and the unemployment insurance commissioners should examine the urgency of amending, during this session, paragraph 3 of section 28 of the act, so as to grant benefits for prolonged periods of unemployment resulting from a labour dispute.
I would be inclined, Mr. Speaker, to go further and even to go beyond the framework of this act. I would also like to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to the advisability of studying the possibility of granting unemployment benefits to the Louiseville strikers, since they have been out of work for several months. I understand that it would create a precedent. However, I believe it would be a humanitarian gesture that would alleviate the sufferings of these people and bring a little sunshine and happiness to the families of Louiseville, where women and children are the innocent victims of that painful experience. As the Christmas season is approaching, it is the nicest gift we could make to the families of the Louiseville workers.
Several strikers also find themselves in an abnormal situation, because at the beginning of the strike they found work elsewhere, worked for several days or even a few months, but are now again unemployed. When they apply for unemployment insurance, they are told that they are not entitled to any benefits because they have not resumed their work. That decision is based on section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
It is an unfortunate situation, because these people have made sacrifices, they have left their home town to take work elsewhere, they have done everything they could to provide for their families, but today they are unable to find work anywhere. They are practically reduced to begging. The situation warrants careful and immediate attention. Knowing the concern of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) for the workers, I am confident that he will take my remarks into serious consideration and I hope that he will find a way of helping those people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like, first, to offer my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Langlois) for the interest he has always taken in the situation, particularly with regard to the painful conditions which have been prevailing in the lovely town of Louiseville for almost nine months.
I am personally aware of the interest shown by the hon. member, who, on several occasions during this long period of time, has sought my advice with a view to finding a solution to the difficult problems which most of those who are affected by this strike must face, or even a remedy to their sufferings. Since the federal government has no jurisdiction in the matter, we have studied together various provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act that might concern these workers. Most of them, as a matter of fact, have been contributing for many years to the unemployment insurance fund and sincerely believe they have claims to assert under this act, since they have been deprived of their livelihood. Unfortunately, as my hon. friend stated, under section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act the payment of benefits to any insured person taking part in or directly affected by a strike or a lock-out is prohibited. The only way to remedy the situation is to introduce an amendment to that effect by an act of parliament.
For my part, I doubt whether it would be wise to recommend payment of unemployment benefits to workers on strike. In doing so, parliament would take sides in a dispute between workers and employers and its action, through its payment of unemployment benefits, would likely help prolong a situation which it is in the interest of all to settle as soon as possible.
As to amending the act by adding to section 28, subparagraph 3, a provision which would take no account of the period of time spent by the striker away from his work, as soon as he has resumed his employment, for the purpose of calculating the 188 contributions which he is supposed to have paid during the two years preceding an eventual application for benefits, I may say to the hon. member, knowing the spirit in which he makes this suggestion and his earnest desire to help

solve some of the problems that might arise, that I am quite willing to give his request most sympathetic attention.
I am not sure how the unemployment insurance commission's advisory committee could see its way clear to accept this request since its granting would inevitably affect the unemployment insurance fund. As it happens this amendment would delay the payment of benefits beyond the limits provided by legislation at this time.
I can assure the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge that I will personally bring to
the notice of the unemployment insurance commission, and through the commissioners, to the notice of the advisory committee, the advisability of exempting an unemployed worker, under the provisions of section 28 of the act, should he have been out on strike in the two years preceding an application for payment of such benefits. This would more particularly apply to the workers at Louise-ville, who against their will have been unemployed for the past nine months.
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add to what I have just said. However, through you, I wish to assure the working population of Louiseville of the interest shown by their representative in this work stoppage which has affected them for so long, and of the interest which the Minister of Labour and myself, as parliamentary assistant, have been continuously taking in the matter for the past nine months. Should the opportunity arise to put an end to the difficulties of the working population of Louiseville, we will gladly avail ourselves of that opportunity and co-operate with the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge.
I most sincerely want this situation to come to an end as soon as possible.
I hope that Christmas will not go by without my hon. friend-should he be unable to obtain for them unemployment insurance benefits-having at least the pleasure of seeing all his constituents resume work under fair and equitable conditions in the best interest of the working population of Louiseville.

Our second largest industry is our fishing and, while some progressive methods have been evolved in later years, I am confident that under the new minister's direction we will experience a revivication, and a complete and thorough study of what the industry has accomplished in the past and what is possible to attain in the future. I now invite the minister to come to the province of Prince Edward Island at the beginning of fishing operations in the coming season to obtain firsthand knowledge of our industry. I will take him to the first fresh filleting and fish meal processing plant in our province, located at Souris in my riding. Our provincial department of industry and natural resources, in conjunction with the federal department, has carried on scientific research work which has proved of great value to the provincial industry. Under the direction of the minister, Hon. Eugene Cullen, and his deputies, this department has surely proven its worth by the results it has already attained in promotional work and advancement for the industry.
I am pleased to note that the speech from the throne indicates that legislation will be implemented to provide some measure of assistance for the rural mail couriers in this country. Provision was made in the session of 1951 for increases to couriers receiving less than $1,000 per annum, and the increases granted to those couriers on application have been generally satisfactory. Now I am confident that the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) will provide, through the coming legislation, liberal increases for those couriers presently underpaid.
To the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) I would suggest that the eligible age for blind pensions be reduced from the present age of 21 years to 16 years, so the blind child may receive assistance from the termination of the family allowance. There is every justification for this because the parents of blind children are subjected to greater costs for education, to make them useful citizens, than in the case with nondefective children. It is my opinion that the means test should be dispensed with for

The Address-Mr. Kickham blind people, and I would like to see the minister remove this impediment to full pensions for the blind.
From listening to the remarks of the hon. junior member for Queens in this house, I am sure his words were not calculated to further advance himself politically in Queens because the Liberal government's public works in that riding are too obvious. The hon. junior member for Queens, for example, cannot place the Charlottetown C.N.R. hotel under his hat; and if he takes himself down to the shore he will see a newly-constructed railway wharf. This work was completed by the Canadian Dredge and Dock Company of Toronto last spring. When he takes a look at the large, commodious frost-proof potato warehouse recently renovated and resting on that spacious wharf, he will see that he cannot put that under his umbrella. All these were constructed by Liberal governments. Further, I understand that the enlargement of the Charlottetown airways in Queens will be proceeded with, and I am sure that if the late J. L. Douglas had lived Charlottetown would now have a spacious public building, provided the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) could release the steel and other materials required for such a building. I can, however, give the junior member for Queens the assurance that it will be built by the Liberals just as soon as supplies are made available and with the backing of the next two Liberal members for Queens, Messrs. Miller and Matheson.
It is my pleasure now to express my thanks to the efficient and friendly Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) on behalf of the people of my constituency and myself for his response to my many requests for construction work on wharves, breakwaters, frostproof potato warehouses and extensions, and the dredging of channels, harbours and rivers to provide more adequate facilities for oceangoing vessels which carry our produce to foreign ports, thus bringing about cheaper freight rates and competition with the government-owned railway. The provisions to assist fishermen at the many fishing points have been of great assistance. There still remains much to be done. We need a new protection work constructed at Murray Harbour north for the protection of fishermen's boats and equipment. At this point boats and valuable equipment are subject to the crippling lashes of the sea. I am confident that an adequate amount will be included in this session's estimates for this very necessary work.
We also need a complete reconstruction job on the government-owned railway wharf at Georgetown. In its present condition the


wharf cannot provide safe accommodation for large boats tying up alongside the frost-proof potato warehouse, and does not provide the proper facilities for loading pulp and pit prop boats. A dredging job is necessary in the inner part of the harbour. An extension to the protection work at Basin Head harbour is also awaiting attention. So far as the public building at Montague is concerned, the necessary building sites have been purchased and are now vested in the crown. An estimate for this building has been passed by the house, and the Department of Public Works will in all probability proceed with the construction in the near future.
Before concluding my remarks on public works, I wish to extend my thanks to the deputy minister and the engineers at Ottawa and Charlottetown. They have at all times extended to me the greatest measure of assistance and co-operation.
With respect to the ferry service to and from our province, it is most imperative that additional services be provided from Wood islands to Caribou and from Borden to Tormentine. I do know that an additional boat for the Wood islands service is being given much consideration by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) inasmuch as I attended a meeting with the minister in that connection last week. So far as the Cape Tormentine-Borden service is concerned, I suggest that if we had a boat to carry passenger and railway freight cars in the summer months this would permit the space now taken up by those cars to be used by automobiles and trucks.
I am confident that if the government realized that new ferry boats were an urgent need at both Wood islands and Borden financial provision would be made at this session for their immediate construction. If the amounts necessary were voted at this session I expect that it would be all of two years before the boats would be ready for service. We are entitled to adequate ferry service under the terms of confederation, and I am sure the people of Canada would not wish to have the smallest province restricted in any way. They want to see our province enjoy the same transportation facilities as are enjoyed by them. We wish to develop and exploit to the fullest measure the tourist industry in order to help to finance the province's road and electricity programs. We need the additional ferries to move our fish and farm produce to export markets. Can one picture the provinces of Quebec and Ontario in our position, not having adequate transportation facilities available to transport tourists and exportable products?

I said in the beginning I was confident that if the government fully realized the situation that now exists it would arouse their gravest concern, with the result that additional transportation facilities would be immediately provided. If the Canadian economy can afford to contribute millions of dollars each year to the Asiatic countries under the Colombo plan, if we can lend and donate millions to Great Britain, surely we can find sufficient funds to provide essential transportation services for Canadians.
The co-operative movement in our province and in the maritimes generally met with a severe loss in the passing of Dr. A. B. MacDonald, one of its pioneers. I knew Dr. MacDonald personally, having met him on numerous occasions in our province during the fourteen years he was associated with Dr. M. M. Coady in the work of St. Francis Xavier university extension department. His boundless energy and devotion to the work of organizing adult study club groups, cooperative producer and consumer groups, credit unions, etc., led him to larger fields of endeavour, and in 1944 co-operative leaders saw the need of a larger and more active national co-operative organization.
Those leaders, knowing of Dr. MacDonald's unsurpassed ability in the field of organization, selected him for the task. Having formed the larger organization, he served as national secretary of the Co-operative Union of Canada until his death on September 13 last at the comparatively early age of 59 years. Dr. MacDonald was a great maritimer. He was a great Canadian. The work he accomplished in teaching the labouring man, the fisherman and the farmer a way to more general prosperity, thus raising his standard of living and giving him greater economic freedom, will ever remain a tribute to his memory.
In closing my remarks I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we had a visitor to our fair isle and he was harsh, by Karsh!

It has to do with the sacrifices of the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker. Canadians are not a martial people. They have shown that when war is forced upon them they are prepared to meet it, and meet it with courage unsurpassed. But we are not a martial people. We do not as a people like to keep standing armies; we do not flaunt any military spirit before the world. It was with a measure of acknowledged reluctance that the Canadian people faced up to what was put before them as the stern necessity for rearmament. They accepted the burdens courageously, but regretfully. And I think, Mr. Speaker, it is only right and proper to say that when they were called upon to face these heavy exactions they expected all their elected representatives in this House of Commons, and all members of the government opposite, would see that every dollar that was taken from the pockets of the people for the purpose of rearmament would be spent carefully for that purpose.
Never has a higher obligation rested upon a parliament, or upon a government, to make sure that every dollar expended for this purpose was carefully and prudently expended, than has rested upon this government and this parliament in connection with this rearmament program.
It was something of the spirit of a crusade that prompted the Canadian people to support Canadian participation in the efforts of the United Nations to withstand aggression in Korea and in the garrisoning of Germany to withstand any possible aggression by the Kremlin in central Europe. Mr. Speaker, what a betrayal of the confidence of the

Canadian people that, in the face of that crusading spirit and in the face of acceptance by the Canadian people of these heavy burdens and exactions for the purpose of providing needed rearmament for this country, the Canadian government has failed so lamentably to see that this money has been carefully and wisely expended!
Mr. Speaker, you will remember that Mr. Currie says in this report that, far more serious than the actual defalcations, and far more serious than the actual amount of materials and goods which have been stolen, is what has been lost to the Canadian people in the proven waste and inefficiency which has been exposed. And what do the Canadian people find? Well, we have had exposures in recent months of colossal waste and extravagance; and now in this report, to cap it all, we find proof of shocking irregularities and of what is, in effect, a whole break-down of the system of supervising expenditure.

It cannot escape its responsibility, in the light of parliamentary practice. And above all, Mr. Speaker, it cannot escape its responsibility to the supreme Canadian people.

I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has anything to do with this matter, but I had hopes last week when I made an appeal to him in his absence to have some justice done. The

only answer we have got so far in my opinion is a cover-up, coupled with the suggestion of a threat which I found very unpleasant. For that reason I come back to it.
I have tried in this house to speak with a certain sense of responsibility, and I never had a greater sense of responsibility than I have now. Yesterday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), to my regret, referred to this as a small matter. I said to him then, and I repeat to him now, that I do not regard justice as a small matter. I regret that it would appear that the attitude of the government-because there has been no other attitude expressed-is that it is a small matter. I still hope this attitude may be changed. I shall try to satisfy the house that the answer that has been given is no answer. If the house should accept that, then I still hope something may be done.
The Minister of Transport spoke more in sorrow than in anger, and wanted to treat me as some kind of erring child. He pointed out to me that I had made a terrible mistake in relying on hearsay. I suppose, in a sense, whatever is in a newspaper is, in the technical, legal sense, for all I know hearsay. After all, the people who are reported in the newspaper do not speak with their own voices. They are reported in the newspaper, and to that extent, in the narrow sense, the minister may be right. However, I do not think we should be bamboozled by the legal jargon, and I suggest that is all the minister was doing. When I asked the minister if he impugned any of the facts on which I based my speech, and which were reported in the Winnipeg Tribune, a responsible newspaper, all the minister said was that it was hearsay and therefore he would pay no attention to it. In my opinion the important thing is whether these facts were true as they were related in the newspaper. I believe they are true. Neither of the ministers appeared to say they were not true; therefore I am entitled to believe that, like me, they believe they are true.

Secondly, I gave as an even stronger reason the impossibility of any sensible person accepting the explanation of the president of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Speaker, along with other members who have spoken in this debate I was amazed at the contents of the Currie report. I think members of parliament generally will regret exceedingly that thefts have prevailed at the Petawawa camp to the extent disclosed by the report, and that there has been such a terrific waste of public funds. The types of thefts are now well known to members of the house. For instance, we hear of such things as the loss of 18,000 bags of cement and 550 tons of so-called scrap iron, part of which turned out to be not scrap at all but kitchen ranges, cannon heaters, shower stalls and sinks. This is something that all of us must regret exceedingly.
Reading through the report I was amazed to learn that there had been the loss of C.P.R. rails, and that immediately this loss was brought to the attention of persons at the camp they proceeded to tear up and steal the rails from the C.N.R. spur line, to replace the C.P.R. rails that had been taken.
It seems to me clear from the report that the responsibility is very definitely that of the Department of National Defence. If the department had been doing its job these thefts would not have taken place. In Mr. Currie's report, as it appears in Hansard at page 712, he says:	.
At Petawawa, however, the crooks were present and took advantage of the situation, and it is an unhappy circumstance that the beginning of this investigation lies not inside the Department of National Defence and its full complement of regulations and supervising personnel, but with the receipt of an anonymous letter.
The Department of National Defence, with its full complement of officers and personnel, was either unwilling or unable to discover that thefts were taking place. Placing the responsibility squarely on the laxity of the Department of National Defence, Mr. Currie goes to say:
It must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions . . . The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
As I have said, the responsibility lies with the government, with the Department of National Defence. Under our system of responsible government, in my opinion the

The Address-Mr. Argue government is unable to make a scapegoat of anyone; because even though it may take action against the wrongdoers, nevertheless in the light of this report it is definitely responsible for having neglected to provide against such a possibility, even after having been warned periodically by the auditor.
This report is dated November 26. As one of the press representatives has said-I believe it was Mr. Blakely in this morning's Gazette-this is the date of the official version. And the date of the authorized version, the other edition, is exactly the same. We have had therefore two versions of this report.
Well, this is not the only report of a government commission of which we may have two versions. Members from Saskatchewan, in particular, have been hoping that the report of a royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river development project would be made public at an early date. We know, from the reply of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to a question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) on Friday, November 21, that the report was ready as early as November 19, except for printing, and that according to a letter received by the Prime Minister from the secretary of the commission it was expected that the printing and publication would take place by December 15.
We are now waiting for the Prime Minister to table that report in the house, so that we may see what is in it. I think we have an inkling already of what it may contain, because Mr. V. J. Mackie, a very responsible member of the press gallery, in an article appearing in the Regina Leader-Post of November 22 had this to say:
The royal commission does not recommend that the proposed irrigation and power project be proceeded with, on the grounds that it would be too costly to undertake at present.
The report will suggest an alternative, but much less ambitious, development of the Saskatchewan river, it was learned.
Well, apparently the experience we have had in regard to the Currie report is being repeated at least to some extent in connection with the report of the royal commission on the South Saskatchewan dam, because as long ago as November 22 this press representative makes a categorical statement as to the main findings of the commission. I think it is the duty of the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to produce the report of that royal commission to this house before the Christmas recess. I can tell the Prime Minister that if the royal ddmmission recommends against the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam members of parliament from western Canada, at

least members of this group, will have something to say about it. We will condemn the abandonment of that project, whether or not the royal commission is in fact recommending against it.
I should like to know if the contents of this article sum up the report of that royal commission. If the report of the royal commission on the South Saskatchewan dam is adverse, then in the light of Liberal promises made in every election since 1935, especially by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I believe it will be found that the Liberal party has lost the confidence of the people of Saskatchewan.
It seems clear to me that with the bringing to light of the Currie report, with its damning evidence against the Department of National Defence, the whole government now lacks the confidence of the Canadian people. I suggest to the government that in view of the Currie report, and particularly if the royal commission should make an adverse recommendation as to the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam, the best thing it can do is go to the people of Canada in a general election at a date as early as is practicable having in view road and weather conditions.

It is a progressive and growing town; it is a town in which new places of business are opening every year, and it should have a federal building.

If the estimates are brought down at this session I suggest in all seriousness to the Minister of Public Works that he include an item for a federal building in Assiniboia. I do not think the people of Canada, at any rate the people of Saskatchewan, are going to return many Liberals to parliament, but no matter; I do feel that the people of Assiniboia are deserving of such a building. The premises now being used for a post office are rented, and a new federal building could be used not only for the post office but for the local detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the federal officials working for the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I want to refer now to what I consider is the plight of agricultural producers, particularly the producers of livestock and dairy

products. I followed with interest the proceedings of the recent dominion-provincial conference on agricultural matters, and I was concerned with the many reports released by officials of the federal government who were attending that conference. According to the Regina Leader-Post of October 24 the Minister of Agriculture stated at a public meeting:
"Our livestock difficulty is not there because of anyone's wish," he said, "but because of foot-and-mouth disease".
Then it continued1:
"If we could keep our livestock on our farms and feed our surplus grain to it we would solve both problems.
I think there is an increasing indication that today livestock prices in Canada are not at a low figure because of foot-and-mouth disease or because of the loss of the United States livestock market. I should like to quote from a press release which was made at the dominion-provincial conference concerning statements made by officials of the federal Department of Agriculture. One statement referring to the United States was as follows:
The number of cattle slaughtered has begun to increase this year with a more rapid rise in prospect for 1953.
And again:
A further easing of prices received by farmers is suggested for 1953 whereas the index of prices paid by farmers will likely be slightly higher.
Referring to the United States market this official states that there is likely to be a further easing of United States cattle prices. Referring to Canada, this press release stated:
A decline in Canadian livestock prices in 1953 from corresponding levels a year ago will probably result from increased marketings and an anticipated further easing of United States prices. This decrease is likely to be more pronounced in cattle and calves than in hogs, with least change in prices of lamb and mutton.
There we have Department of Agriculture officials saying that 1953 will see a further lowering of cattle and livestock prices in Canada. There has been a terrific fall in livestock prices in Canada from the autumn of 1951 until the present time, and the best prospect officials of the minister's own department can hold out is that Canadian livestock prices will go down even further. Dealing with the farmer's general income position in relation to his 1952 income, the press release had this to say:
Although farm cash income from the sale of farm products and from participation payments may reach a new all-time high, it is estimated that a lower income in kind, reduced values of year-end inventory changes and higher operating costs will serve to provide a net farm income about 5 per cent below a year ago.
The forecast is that farm net income for 1952 will be 5 per cent below farm net income in 1951. It goes on to say that farm
The Address-Mr. Argue income is also expected to be somewhat lower in 1953. In other words the position of the farmer is worsening. Even though the United States market will be opened on March 1 the officials of the minister's department hold out no hope for an increase in livestock prices. In fact they say that there will be a further decrease in Canadian livestock prices. The Financial Post of December 13 contained an article on the front page entitled: "Cattle Prices May go Down, Won't Lift With U. S. Ban."
It says:
Thousands of Canadian farmers who are planning to withhold their cattle from the home market in anticipation of higher prices when the United States embargo comes off March 1 may be in for a rude shock. Unless there is a big change in the next two months, and top beef authorities in both countries cannot see it now, Canadian farmers will be forced to take sizable cuts in most cattle prices to get into the big United States market, cuts that could make today's domestic prices look pretty attractive. On the basis of today's prices, for instance, Canada could market only one class of beef cattle in the United States, choice steers. That class represents some 5 per cent to 10 per cent of total normal marketings in this country. None of the big volume cattle types could lay down competitively in the United States after freight, tariff, brokerage and exchange. Here is the current price differential.
Then follow figures with respect to the differential between Canadian and United States cattle prices. If the embargo were lifted now Canadian choice steers, red label beef steers, probably would go up by $1.30 a hundredweight. Good steers probably would go down by $4.30. Canadian commercial steers would drop $5.35 a hundredweight. Commercial cows, good, would drop $2.50 a hundredweight; utility cows would drop $1.80 a hundredweight and canner cows would drop $1.50 a hundredweight. The article to which I have referred shows that the opening of the United States market now to permit Canadian cattle to go into that country and United States cattle to come into Canada would have the effect of lowering Canadian beef prices instead of raising them.
Therefore before the Christmas recess begins I should like an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) of his statement that the only trouble with the livestock industry today is the fact that the United States market has been closed. I should like an explanation of his statement that the thing for farmers to do to solve our surplus grain problem and our inadequate livestock market is to feed our livestock on the farms. If the farmers keep back, as they have been asked by the minister to do, increased numbers of livestock on the farms at the present time, the only effect that can possibly have is a further lowering of prices

The Address-Mr. Argue when these livestock are placed on the market some months from now. I have here a Canadian Press dispatch from Winnipeg dated December 11, which reads:
United States cattle prices are due for a 20 per cent slump in the next four years as beef on the hoof nears 100 million, highest production level in the country's history, Wayne Darrow, president of Farm Reports Incorporated, Washington, said today. In Winnipeg to address the Winnipeg stock exchange annual meeting, Mr. Darrow said in an interview the United States herds are reproducing so fast the American population gain can't keep up.
We have had a dominion-provincial conference on farm matters, and the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture's own officials are almost consistently gloomy. They are forecasting lower livestock prices and a lower net income for agricultural producers. In view of the difficulty we are having in finding adequate markets for beef, pork, cheese, eggs and poultry products, I think the Minister of Agriculture owes it to the house and to the country to make a statement in parliament outlining the position of the agri-;ultural industry and advising our agricultural producers as to what they should do in order to receive the highest possible return in the coming year. I have in my hand the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin for Thursday, December 11. In it there is one paragraph headed, "Drop in Index Number of Farm Prices of Agricultural Products in October", which reads as follows:
Canada's index number of farm prices of agricultural products dropped in October to 243-5-
Mark this.
-the lowest monthly standing since April, 1948.
Farm product prices in October of this year were at their lowest point since April, 1948. While farm prices have been going down since April, 1948, farm costs have been .ncreasing at an alarming rate. In 1949, for example, the index number of farm prices of igricultural products was 255-4 while the 'armers' cost of production index was 204-1. in 1950 the agricultural prices index was !60-8 while the farm costs index was 210-4. in 1951 the index of prices of agricultural products for the whole year was 296 * 9 while ;he index of farm costs was 229-9. For October of this year the index number of 'arm prices of agricultural products was 243 [DOT] 5 while the index of farm costs was 543 -4.
In other words, according to those figures )f the dominion bureau of statistics Canadian igricultural producers on a relative basis are n exactly the same position now as they were n the base period of 1935-39. I say that when igriculture is now placed in the position in which it was from 1935 to 1939 it is becoming i depressed industry; and it is becoming a

depressed industry because of the policies or lack of policies of this government. Of course members of the cabinet get up and brag about employment statistics, the high national income, the very large gross national product, and they say we have prosperity throughout Canada. There may be prosperity throughout Canada today, but we are rapidly approaching a situation where there may be general prosperity for all but the agriculture industry, which may face a depression.
When the agricultural index figures show that agricultural product prices for October of this year are no better than the prices of agricultural products based on costs of production in the period from 1935 to 1939, then agriculture in Canada is not in a very healthy position. On January 1 the Minister of Agriculture is going to drop the support price of hogs by $3 a'hundredweight, from $26 to $23. The government are following a policy of cutting floor prices to the very bottom in the hope that they may prevent full production by the agricultural industry. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) tells us every time we ask for an increase in the old age pension or the family allowance, or every time anyone suggests that the government should reduce taxes, that the only hope of increased services or decreased taxes is through greater production in Canada, a real increase in the gross national product. While the Minister of Finance is telling Canadians that they must work harder and produce more the Minister of Agriculture is telling the farmers, by the actions he takes, that he is afraid of their production. He wants them to cut hog production, beef production, poultry production, right down the line.
There was one reference during the dominion-provincial agricultural conference that did not appear so bleak. At one point one of the economists said that the future may not be too bad for the Canadian turkey industry. He pointed out that turkey prices are away down this fall, and said that no doubt turkey producers are going to cut production to such an extent that those that stay in the business can expect higher prices next year. I believe that is a bankrupt policy if I ever heard one.
I do not commend a minister very often, but I want to commend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the government upon the fact that we have, and have had now for a number of years, a Canadian wheat board handling the marketing of all western grain. No party has more consistently supported the Canadian wheat board than the party to which I have the honour to belong. I want to say that I appreciate a statement made by the Minister

of Trade and Commerce when he spoke to the investment dealers' association of Canada in Toronto on October 28 of this year. I wish the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would study that address very carefully, and I wish he would apply to the rest of the agricultural industry the same type of provision that is now made for the grain producers of western Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say:
In a year like the present, when handling facilities are congested, you can well imagine what an advantage it is for one marketing agency to have full control over the main western grain crops, and to be able to sell them and move them to market as opportunity arises.
He went on to say that the wheat board had successfully marketed last year's crop much of which was of a very low grade, and that this was one of the most remarkable achievements in the history of the grain trade. At another point he said:
-I believe that the wheat board has been able to handle the western crop, during the war and since the war, more successfully than it could have been handled by any other marketing method.
The minister pointed out that because of the way the wheat board is operated, all the producers in any given year get exactly the same price for a given grade of grain. I do not need to repeat that I support the Canadian wheat board and the wheat board system of marketing grain. I should like to see the Minister of Agriculture and this government set up a livestock board or agricultural products board along the lines of the Canadian wheat board, to assemble such agricultural products as beef, dairy and poultry products going into interprovincial and export trade, set a proper initial price and pay the farmers the same prices for the products after the year is completed and the final payment is made.
I see that my time is going, Mr. Speaker, and I have an amendment to move. In order to protect myself against loss of time I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following:
"(f) To recommehd legislation providing for the payment to producers, in respect of farm-stored grain, of an advance equal to 75 per cent of the initial price as established at August 1 in each crop year."
A few days ago I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he would consider making such an advance payment. He said that such a payment was not needed this year because the farmers had marketed more grain this year than in the same period last year, and they were receiving total final payments amounting to $158 million. I want to point out to the minister and to
The Address-Mr. Argue the house just what this final payment means to the average wheat producer.
According to the 1951 census there were 248,716 occupied farms in the three prairie provinces. As reported in the last grain statistics weekly, the grain marketed up to November 27 of this crop year amounted- this is my estimate on the basis of initial prices-to $335 million. This works out to an average income for the western farmer from the sale of grain of $1,350. Participation payments for each farmer averaged $630. This meant that up until that time a farmer had received or was about to receive in payments on grain, both the initial payment and the final payment, something in the neighbourhood of $2,000 each. This is a small gross income, out of which the farmer has to pay his living expenses; his land taxes; pay for machinery; for petroleum products, and the other costs. Certainly this indicates that the average farmer needs some other provision, which I suggest should be an advance payment on farm-stored grain.
I have heard it said, Mr. Speaker, by various members over a cup of coffee that the western farmer is rolling in money; that the Saskatchewan farmer has never made more money in his history. I have heard it said that if you want to find the western farmers in the wintertime go to California, Florida or Texas; and if you cannot find them all there you may find a few of them in British Columbia. Apparently a lot of eastern people believe that the average farmer in Saskatchewan has three or four sections of land, has modern equipment, works a few months a year and spends the winters in the southern United States. I have the census figures which illustrate the size of farms in Saskatchewan. I find that of the various categories of farms by far the largest number were in the category between 240 and 399 acres. I find that 29,000 farmers in Saskatchewan out of 112,000 operated a farm equal to a half section of good land or three-quarters of a section, one-quarter of which was not entirely under cultivation. Farmers who owned more than five quarters of good arable land amounted to only 8 per cent of the total number of farmers. The farmers of western Canada are on the whole not large land owners but farmers with a half or three-quarters of a section, and it is in the interests of the vast majority of farmers that I am proposing this further subamendment.
I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that United States farmers are able to obtain a loan on farm-stored grain. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that the banks will lend the farmers money. I saw a statement in the Regina Leader-Post, I believe
790	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Low it was about November 30, in which the bank officials said they were prepared to lend money on farm-stored grain provided the grain was in good condition and the farmer was in a sound financial position. I am afraid not all those farmers about whom I have been talking, because 80 per cent or more are relatively small farmers, would be able to convince the banks that they were in a sound financial position.
In this proposal, I am not asking for any money from the federal treasury. I am asking for legislation to make provision for the advancing of money on farm-stored grain. I believe it is the best security in the world, and I believe the farmers would be prepared to pay a nominal rate of interest to cover all the costs involved.
Another reason I feel such a proposition should be implemented is the further fact that the farmer is perhaps not the person who suffers most when he cannot sell his grain. The person who suffers greatly, in my opinion, is the businessman in our small communities. A farmer may owe $1,000 or $2,000. A small businessman may have on his books $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000. He knows the accounts are good. The grain is in the bins. But the farmers are unable to sell their grain as rapidly as they would wish and for that reason are unable to speedily pay their accounts.
I moved a similar amendment last year. At that time the hon. member for The Battle-fords (Mr. Bater) moved a subamendment. That subamendment wiped out almost all of my amendment, certainly that part of it in which I was interested. His amendment thanked the government for everything they had done for the farmer. That was fine. This amendment I am now moving is a subamendment and, as I understand the rules, we shall have an opportunity to vote on the subamendment. I ask the hon. members from western Canada, particularly those from Saskatchewan, no matter to which party they may belong, to consider this amendment carefully. I submit that they should vote for it on the basis of the advantage which will accrue to the people they represent.

Mr. Speaker, I have not yet had an opportunity of saying a word about the Currie report, for two reasons. The first and most important one is that I had already exhausted the time I had under the subamendment which we had moved. I therefore could not speak again until now. The second is that I wanted to read the report most carefully and to weigh as calmly and as carefully as possible every word in it, in pursuance of the request made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)


yesterday. I have now given it as much consideration as I can in the time I have had, and I should like just to sum up briefly the attitude I take toward it.
I think there are three things more particularly about which I find myself concerned, and I believe these will be the things that will concern the people of the country as well. The first is that the report is full of evidence that what we told the government two years ago was correct. On several occasions we warned the government that they would have to use vision and foresight, and that they would have to make careful provision against possible wrongdoing, graft and dishonesty because their defence effort was growing bigger every year and would therefore offer greater opportunity for these evils.
The people of the country are certainly going to be greatly alarmed over the evidence of lack of vision and foresight on the part of top or near-top officials of government, as revealed in the report. The government must have known that the bigger the defence effort, the greater would be the opportunity for waste, dishonesty and graft. To me it is surprising-and I suppose it will be surprising to everyone in the country who thinks about it-that, under the circumstances, the government did not see fit to place in responsible positions of authority first-class administrators with adequate training so they could administer the billions of dollars that are being spent and see to it that a system was provided that would prevent waste and graft. Civil administrators of top ability were not appointed and placed in proper positions, although adequate warning came from this side of the house on various occasions. The government therefore really has no excuse.
The second thing about which the people are going to be greatly concerned is this. There are plenty of indications that officials in responsible positions have winked at and continue to wink at evidence of wrongdoing; and they continue to do this until the accumulation of irregularities grows so big as to excite the public in the area in which they have occurred to make complaints and ask for an investigation. In the report of Mr. Currie there seems to be plenty of evidence that a breakdown of morality followed a breakdown of watchfulness and control in the Department of National Defence. If a blind eye continues to be turned toward the serious breaches of regulations, the question most of us ask is this: how long will it be until the whole administration is shot through with immorality? That is the big issue. The government should crack down hard on those who are guilty; and in doing so they must not overlook the people in top positions. They are guilty. There is no question about that.

The third thing I found that concerned me greatly was the situation with which we are confronted when anyone would attempt to tamper with royal commission reports, to change them in order to soften the impact of the findings on the people concerned. I think it is a shocking situation that has been laid bare here in these past two days, and the taxpayers of the country will not be insensible to the fantastic things that have been revealed. I cannot reach any other conclusion in connection with this matter than that the government must take the full responsibility. Inasmuch as that is so, it seems to me that I must add my voice to the voices of those who have already asserted that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) ought to resign.
Perhaps there are others who ought to resign along with him. It is that subject that I should like to talk about for the next few minutes. What I have to say now, Mr. Speaker, was occasioned by a speech made in this house on the evening of December 4, to which I have not yet had a chance to reply.
I should like to refer in a general way to the speech that was made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) that evening. The case he made then was sound, wholly sound. I should like to emphasize the fact that his arguments appeared at that time to register with some of his frightened Liberal colleagues in this house, but they certainly fell flat in Alberta. The people out there are well enough informed that speeches like the one the minister made serve only to convince them that they have made a serious mistake in sending down to parliament a man who cannot do a better job than he did on that occasion.
To all of us who watched the minister as he delivered his speech it was quite evident that the arguments that were written into it did not appeal greatly even to him. He says he wrote it himself. He therefore will have to take full responsibility for it and for what I have to say. I think he might learn that ghost-writers can be a terrible handicap. The beggars are never around to take the rap when the rap comes. Perhaps we should not be too severe on the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys because giving that speech was likely one of the prices he had to pay to his party for the privilege of being Alberta's only cabinet minister.
These things seem to carry their price tags, especially in the Liberal party. This past summer I saw the minister's buddy doing some chore-boy footwork for the party around various communities in the Peace river country. That was likely to pay off his debt for the security he obtained. I am speaking now of the senator from Alberta. It
The Address-Mr. Low must have seemed queer to the house to watch the spectacle of a minister of the crown in this parliament firing the first gun in the Peace River election campaign, a constituency that is over 300 miles from his own constituency of Edmonton West. Hon. members did not know that the minister had been laying the groundwork for that campaign for over a year.
This was not the first instance. I want to give the background to measure what he had to say, because one has to have it. Early this year the minister went to the radio bureau in Ottawa requesting the right to participate in the free -time reports from parliament hill over the radio station in the Peace river country, and he based his demand on the argument that there were certain people in a remote part of his constituency of West Edmonton who could not be reached over the two Edmonton stations, although no part of his riding is more than a few miles from those stations while the station in Grande Prairie is 340 miles from the farthest elector in the West Edmonton constituency. Well, he got the time over the air, and he has been sharing that free time with me over station CFGP in Grande Prairie. Therefore it was not surprising, sir, that the minister carried his Peace River campaign into this house. But what is surprising and almost beyond belief is that a responsible minister of the federal government, the only one Alberta has down here, would rise in his place in this house and make such utterly irresponsible statements as he did a week ago last Thursday night.
People have a right to the truth, particularly from men in the responsible position of ministers of the crown.

I will examine that in minute detail, and we shall let the people judge for themselves on the basis of the facts and the evidence, not just hearsay, or what some ghost-writer puts in.
The minister showed himself to be more irresponsible than any other minister in my experience, Mr. Speaker, and I have seen a lot of them come and go. I am going to say that his speech was full of half-truths and misrepresentations. There were at least two distortions, out of all semblance to their real selves; and there was one statement-well, I do not say it was a complete distortion, Mr. Speaker, it was totally wrong. The minister must have had his green spectacles on when he read what I heard him say here on the 25th day of November, because he did not seem to know that I did not say that his trip to the Peace river was a casual one. I never made any such statement at any time. I did
792	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Low say that he had gone up there to attend a nominating convention, and at that nominating convention made certain statements and cast some rather serious personal aspersions, one of which was that I was not sincere. Well, I was answering that, and the speech he gave the other night in the house was an answer to what I said. I will not take much time to deal with the minister's transparent effort-and it was a transparent effort -to belittle me and hold me up to ridicule.
I am of course grateful to the minister for revealing this far ahead what kind of personal attack he and his Liberal party will launch against me in the federal election campaign next year. You know, it is a good thing to know ahead, because good strategy says: find out what your enemy wants you to do and just do not do it. I thank him for letting me know of it. The only thing he and his party can find to criticize in the eight years I have represented the Peace River constituency is that I do not live there.
The minister says the people of that district are becoming very much aware of the fact that they should have a member of their own community representing them. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals up in Peace River and the minister over the radio are doing their level best to whip up that kind of sentiment by every means, fair or foul, they can think of. Let me make it clear that I have never at any time felt that the people of the Peace river country could not find plenty of individuals amongst themselves who are perfectly capable of representing them in this house; but I did not seek the nomination, and I would like the minister to know that. I did not seek the nomination in Peace River;
I was invited, and I was strongly pressed and urged by the people up there to let my name stand for nomination both in 1945 and in 1949. And I will just tell the minister something else that he seems to forget. In 1945 when the people of the Peace river country held their Social Credit nominating convention I was not even there. I was nominated in absentia, and was notified by telegram that that had been done.
In the intervening years I believe that I have served the people of the constituency well. Most electors up there admit that every section and every corner of the vast constituency, one of the biggest in Canada if not the biggest, have seen me, their Social Credit member, more often and more regularly than they have ever seen their other representatives, including the Liberal ones they have had. I have made a sustained and conscious effort to do my duty to those I represent, and from the evidence I found on my most recent journey through that great constituency the 

vast majority of the people up there have appreciated the efforts I have made and the service I have earnestly tried to give them.
It is true that I live in Ottawa, but so does every other party leader; but of course the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys did not want to be fair about that and grant me the same privilege he grants to his own party leader and to other party leaders as well. He claims, of course, that he lives in Edmonton. The fact is that he lives in Ottawa and continues to own a home in south Edmonton. Let me make it abundantly clear that I do not begrudge him owning that home. If he owned three I would say we ought to be glad we live in a country where people can own three homes if they want to. I say that is his own right, and he does live in Ottawa to carry on his work; but not many of us, sir, can afford two homes. Most of us have a hard enough time to carry the expenses of one home; but those of us who are called to party leadership find that we must live in Ottawa to be able to faithfully and efficiently do the work that devolves upon us. Of course it would hardly be expected that the minister would be moved by any feelings of justice and fairness in such matters, inasmuch as some political advantage might be lost if he did so.
I should like to turn for just a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to some of the particulars of the speech the minister gave, because I want to substantiate what I said at the beginning that his speech was full of half-truths, told as if they were whole truths, misrepresentations and distortions; and if I cannot do this then I shall proceed in the minister's presence to eat this whole Hansard.

In the first place I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the minister seemed to be very concerned about the Peace river country, and he spoke very well about it. I was glad to hear him say the wonderful things he did, because it is a great country. But I am interested in this particular thing. They say that in 1492 Columbus discovered America; in 1952 it appears that the Liberals have discovered the Peace river. That is most interesting to me. He told some very interesting things about the Peace river country. I do not know why, but he got it mixed up with British Columbia building a little connecting highway from very near the Alberta border to Prince George. At any rate, he said the people of the Peace river district looked forward to the day when they could have rail transportation to the Pacific coast. Well, I say, "Yes", just as I did when

the minister was speaking. They certainly do look forward to that. Let me point out just a few things that perhaps the minister has not reviewed.
In the election campaign of 1925 the prime minister and leader of the Liberal party promised an Edmonton audience that the Liberal party would make the Peace River country the spearhead of that party's program. That was in 1925. Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King assured a lot of Peace River people that that would be done. There were a lot of Peace River people at the Edmonton meeting and the Liberals wanted a Liberal member up there, you see. In the 1926 campaign this same Liberal leader told a similar audience in Edmonton that he would build a coast outlet to the Peace river country as soon as it was humanly possible-to get votes, of course. Then when the 1930 election campaign got under way Mr. Mackenzie King told another Edmonton political gathering that he would support the construction of a railway from the Peace river country to the Pacific coast within one year, if the railway companies failed to build a coast outlet within the year. At about the same time Sir Henry Thornton, then president of the Canadian National Railways, said that when grain shipments from the Peace river country reached 10 million bushels per year, the railway from the Peace river to the coast would be built.
Well, this is the final month of 1952, and that great country of the mighty Peace is in much the same position with regard to rail transportation as it was in 1925, except that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) has again said that the Peace river country ought to have a railway to the coast.
Twenty-seven years of promises, broken Liberal promises, are all the people of my constituency have had, and no rail outlet westward is in sight even yet, despite the fact that the total yearly grain production has reached almost four times the 10 million bushels that were held by the president of the C.N.R. to be necessary before his company would begin building that railroad.
My constituency of Peace River does, indeed, need a rail outlet to the coast. The vast majority of the people out there have no confidence whatever in Liberal promises.	So they are prepared to support a movement that has demonstrated that it just does not go around at election time making idle promises. They know that a Social Credit government at Ottawa would have that railway between
The Address-Mr. Low Hines Creek and Dawson Creek extended to Prince Rupert and/or Vancouver in its first term of office.
The Peace river country is even now one of the greatest food producing, timber producing and mineral producing areas in America; and the 65,000 people up there are entitled to better treatment than they have had at the hands of a Liberal government here in Ottawa. They are carrying a transportation burden away beyond their ability to bear, and certainly away beyond what they should bear.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys made a statement in connection with conservation in Alberta. He claimed there was no conservation being carried on, and then he said:
One place in Alberta where conservation is being practised is on the important eastern slopes of the Rockies where under a federal-provincial arrangement a splendid timber and water conservation program is being carried out. In this case, under the joint agreement, the federal government is contributing the major share of the required funds, close to $4 million to date.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I admit that there is a very, very wonderful joint conservation program going on. I admit openly, and have done for many years, right before this House of Commons, that the eastern slope of the Rockies agreement is a splendid agreement. But what the minister does not tell the people, when he makes reference to this matter, is that for a good many years Alberta carried the total cost of preserving the watershed on the eastern slope of the Rockies, which gives rise to interprovincial waters and therefore becomes essentially a federal matter.

I am given to understand by those who prepared the cases for trial that it became quite apparent that those

men who were convicted had determined that they would use their positions to further their personal ends, and that they were able to do so not so much because of the system being inadequate as because they had determined to circumvent the system, and to falsify the records in some cases.
Everyone knows that in any large undertaking where responsibility, as a matter of necessity, must be delegated to a great many persons, unless you can rely upon the honesty of those who are in the higher positions no system, however well it may be designed, will prevent misappropriations. It is to be noted in this connection that no shortages have occurred since these men have been removed. According to the Currie report itself, no shortages have occurred in other camps where honest men are in control, even under the same accounting system. I am sure, therefore, that where defaults have occurred through these human frailties of trusted employees it behooves all of us, in fairness to those who are naturally affected by the Currie report, to withhold judgment on whether the system was entirely bad until there has been an opportunity of having this matter brought before the committee on defence expenditures, and in this way hearing all the relevant facts concerning the whole matter.
My purpose in intervening in this debate, sir, is to examine and discuss certain statements made by a number of opposition speakers, particularly of the official opposition and notably the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), to the effect that this government has been imposing unduly high taxes upon the Canadian people. In the welter of broad statements and generalities, most of which do not even glitter, I suggest that the best way, and indeed the only accurate way, in which this question can be satisfactorily determined is to place upon the record the plain facts so the Canadian people may judge, from those facts, whether they have been called upon to carry a heavier load of taxation than that of citizens of comparable countries.
I should like to start out with those facts upon which, in my judgment, the government and the Conservative opposition at least- and perhaps the other opposition parties- seem to be in agreement. I think we agree that, by and large, government expenditures, no matter how wise and proper they are, must be paid for by taxation. Therefore the main factors in determining the amount of taxes which Canadians have to pay are Canadian policies which involve the expenditure of money. Are the government and the official opposition agreed upon those policies involving the expenditure of money? If we can take
The Address-Mr. Garson at their face value the statements made by the members of the official opposition, I think the answer to that question is yes.
Let me illustrate this point by quoting from the words of the Leader of the Opposition himself as set out in his interesting and useful speech at the beginning of this debate, which may be found at pages 20 and 21 of Hansard. To begin with he agreed-and I think this is true of every member of the opposition and of every member of all parties-with the wisdom of Canada's foreign policy and the need for military preparedness which is an integral part of that policy. The Leader of the Opposition made this abundantly clear in language which I think we would all endorse. I will not go into the details of everything he said, but he clinched the point when he said:
Canadians are I am sure all ready to pay the taxes that are really necessary to defend our freedom.
There seems no doubt, therefore, that the opposition fully supports the military preparedness program of the government and any expenditures and taxes which are really necessary to carry it out.
