I should like to say in relation to these tables, in order to be fair with all members, that the changes in the exchange rates of the various currencies which are involved, all of which have been noted in the tables, make some comparisons difficult, and may sometimes unavoidably distort the true picture to some extent, but these distortions do not affect the validity of the use to which I propose to put these figures, nor the conclusions which I am going to ask hon. members to draw from them.
Mr. Speaker, what do these figures show? Well, the first point that stands out in all these tables is that personal exemptions in Canada are much higher than those in any of these other countries. This means that the great mass of Canadians in the low income brackets bear a much smaller rate of income tax than do the mass of citizens in any of the other countries named, and particularly those citizens in the low income brackets in countries like New Zealand and the United Kingdom, where Labour party social welfare and other policies have been the major factor in determining the tax patterns which the present governments of those countries have inherited from their Labour predecessors. Even Labour governments cannot solve the financial problem of paying for heavy welfare costs by soaking the rich. Unhappily, there are not enough rich to soak, to begin with; and when they are too heavily soaked they cease to be rich.
Next they show that during the wartime peak, Canadian taxes were the lowest of all these countries on incomes up to $2,000 a year. Above $2,000 a year Canada's income taxes were somewhat higher than those of the United States, but they were appreciably lower than those of the United Kingdom, Australia or New Zealand throughout the whole range of incomes.
Now, what about the post-war low, when the war was over and taxes went down or were reduced in all these countries? How does the Canadian post-war low compare? The Canadian post-war low tax upon a married taxpayer with no dependents was the lowest of all of these countries on incomes up to $5,000. On incomes above that level Canada's taxes were higher than those of the United States but considerably lower than those of the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.
Well then, after our taxes had been reduced in all these countries, and we were making a good recovery when the war was over, Korea occurred. Then all these countries had to impose taxation in order to defend freedom and to meet the threat of aggression. And at the high point of the post-Korea
The Address-Mr. Garson period, Canada's personal income taxes were the lowest of any of these countries on incomes up to $5,000. Above that level they were somewhat higher than those of the United States, but much lower than those of all the other countries named.
Now, most important of all, what about present taxes, the taxes which we are told by all members of the opposition are such an inordinate burden upon the Canadian people? At the present time, of all these countries I have named, Canada's taxes are lowest on all incomes up to $5,000. Above that level they are much lower than all the other countries except the United States. In other words, at all these periods the burden of Canadian taxes compares very favourably indeed with that of other comparable countries in the English-speaking world.

Bravo.
Resale price maintenance has absolutely nothing to do with it.

Moreover there is every indication of a further substantial increase between 1951 and 1952. For example, the total wages and salaries, which is a large component of personal income comprising upon the average more than 60 per cent, was 12 per cent higher for the first eight months of 1952 than for the comparable period of 1951. I suggest that the only base upon which our hon. friends are able to argue-I must say that having a very poor case they make a good fist of it indeed-is that although we impose in this country rates of taxation which compare very favourably with other comparable countries, the economic results of government policies in Canada and of the great amount of effort put forward by the Canadian people are so favourable that these tax rates, applied to the national income of the country, produce the surpluses of which my hon. friends complain. They not only have done that but they have enabled Canadians in the period since the war to invest in this country about $16 billion of money in all sorts of additions to Canada's productive capacity. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that one of the main reasons these investments, to the extent of about 85 per cent I believe, are made by Canadians, and the balance by outsiders investing their money in Canada, are the very surpluses and reduction of debt concerning which certain opposition members are always complaining.

(Mr. Garson.]

confidence, not necessarily in the government but in the steadiness and reliability of the Canadian people, because they had seen the Canadian people over quite a period of time now-too long, I know for our friends in the opposition-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -steadily support a courageous and honest government financial policy which, by keeping our budget in balance and reducing our national debt, thereby guaranteed the safety not only of this new $16 billion worth of investments but of all the existing investments and properties of the Canadian people as well. If we had not followed this policy, does any reasonable man suppose there would have been that confidence in this country, in our dollar, in our prospects and the like, that would have brought about this amount of investment? Perhaps some of these investments would have been made. But I suggest that the majority would not, for the simple reason that not one of us in this chamber would want to take his own money and invest it in a country in which even in good times the government was going perennially into debt year after year without making any attempt to properly balance its budget. These investments constitute by far the largest single increase in Canada's productive capacity that has ever taken place in our history.
The government is floundering.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

For that reason they are
enormously important to every single Canadian. The hard fact is that all our wages, our pensions, our social welfare benefits, all the arms that protect our liberty and the whole of our standard of living come from one source only, the production of goods and services by Canadians. They come from that source not only for us but for our children and for our grandchildren. Therefore anything that, to the extent of $16 billion of investment, increases that production benefits every Canadian, the big shots and the little shots alike. Whatever my share of this total national production may be, I am bound to benefit if the national production is increased.
All this has been done, may I suggest to my hon. friends, especially to the official opposition and particularly to the financial critic of that party, at no real cost to our present standard of living. Let me quote a question which was asked in that great Conservative paper, the Winnipeg Tribune, by a highly intelligent correspondent who, as it happens, is a professor of economics at the University of Manitoba.
What is his name?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Professor Barber. He said:
Would you agree that the $2 billion surplus which the dominion government has managed to build up over the past five years has not meant the loss of an equivalent amount of goods to the Canadian people? In fact, even if the dominion government had reduced taxes during this period by $2 billion and thus wiped out its surplus entirely, there would not have been one more car, house or suit of clothes available to the Canadian people.
Accordingly, if it is possible to reduce the national debt without in any way reducing the real income or real welfare of the Canadian people, why is this such an undesirable policy?
It is no wonder then, Mr. Speaker, that, except for a small minority of Canadians who hope to pick up a few votes by misrepresenting the achievements of their own country, there is a very clear understanding today amongst all competent judges throughout the whole world that the Canadian people since the war have done an absolutely magnificent job of handling their economy.
The people, but not the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Obviously the greatest part of the credit for this achievement must go where it belongs, to the Canadian people and producers; but it is also a fact that none of the sophistries of my hon. friends can disprove that if government policies had not been as courageous and realistic-

Actually, Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate again, but in view of some of the statements that have been made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) I felt compelled to make some reply. This is especially so, because of the references he made to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). I do this with regret, because I think hon. members in this house are getting fed up with listening, day in and day out, to the type of propaganda that has been dished out by the Social Credit group in dealing with provincial matters. They have even gone so far as to obtain statements from the premier of Alberta to refute a statement made in this house by a cabinet minister.

I am sorry the hon. member for Peace River is not in his seat tonight. Among the phrases that have been used with reference to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, as I have them noted, was one to the effect that the people of Alberta made a mistake in sending a man like that to Ottawa. I think Alberta is fortunate in having here a man of the calibre of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, and we respect him for his honesty and his sincerity. The hon. member referred to the minister's statements as being utterly irresponsible; half truths; misrepresentations and distortions, and so on. One could add to those some of the statements the hon. member made in this house quite recently, such as master of smear technique; master of evasion; questionable methods, bandit leaders; stinkers in high places. These are the type of phrases used by a gentleman who is not only the leader of a political party, but who aspires to become the prime minister of Canada.
I notice that some of you are smiling, and some of you are laughing. You may think this is funny, but the leader of the Social Credit party doesn't think so. Let me quote a press report appearing in the Edmonton Journal of November 27, 1952. The headline is "Solon Low sees possibility of federal control by Social Credit." The article reads in part:
Solon E. Low, national leader of the Social Credit party, said Wednesday he would not be surprised if his party controls the Commons at Ottawa after the next federal election.
Farther down the article reads:
"I do not mean to boast that we will become the government, but I am not ruling out anything", he said. "It is possible".
Then the hon. member goes on to give three reasons why he thinks this party will control the House of Commons or form the government. One of the reasons he cited was the result of the British Columbia election. The second reason was the result of the Alberta election. As to his third reason, I quote from the article:
"On top of that, Premier Manning made a triumphant tour of eastern Canada-not for political purposes but to do a job in religion". He added: "It has its political implications. It will hold implications for us (the party), I am sure".
He said political writers read into the premier's trip political significance, which was not designed.
"It will have that effect, but that is not what he went east for", he reiterated. "But if a man does a good thing, and it rebounds to the good of the political movement he leads, I am not going to deny it".
The hon. gentleman feels he is probably coming to Ottawa to form the next government. He has made a reference to highways, and has introduced a statement by Premier Manning of Alberta. Let me read to you,


Mr. Speaker, an editorial appearing in the Calgary Herald of April 17, 1952. I believe nobody would accuse the Calgary Herald of being a Liberal paper. The heading oi this editorial is "Millions of dollars for potholes". I shall read the editorial:
The province of Alberta intends to spend $24,400,000 for highways this year but if the examples of past highway construction are to be the criterion of future development, the money is just being wasted.
You heard what was quoted tonight in the letter from Premier Manning of Alberta. To continue:
There may be 1,200 miles of paved road in Alberta today, but great chunks of it are no better than plowed fields right now because of the spring thaws. That is a lot of baloney.
Sit down.

I am sorry-

One would have thought that, after years of experience with climatic conditions here and the experiments on soil which have been carried on at the university of Alberta, the highways department would have learned a few lessons in the art of road building. It surely should have realized, as even Alberta cities are beginning to realize, that you can't just roll a bit of pavement on the prairie and expect it to last. Hence when the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys made the statement that the roads in Alberta are just like the Social Credit party, with a fine surface and very little foundation, this editorial bears him out. It continues:
It should experiment on materials to find the best ones to combat Alberta's continual freezing and thawing weather. It should learn to build wide, solid highways, not long, narrow collapsible ones.
But then, we suppose, the highways department isn't allowed to be interested in building roads, but must make sure that it builds votes instead. It must allocate its expenditures (and therefore establish its specifications) to construct the mostest with the least. It must see that some pavement gets into the good Social Credit constituencies, even if it means skimping elsewhere. Thus the province can expand its mileage while retaining low grade standards.
That sum of $24,400,000 is an awful lot of money to sink in the paved mudholes Alberta is getting. When will the government begin to use these moneys properly and efficiently?

Mr. Speaker, as I say it is with considerable regret that I rise and deal with these matters on the floor of this house.
I would not mind listening to a lot of this propaganda coming from the Social Credit group if only they were consistent. Referring again to the hon. member for Peace River, may I say that he was one of the first members of the Social Credit group in 1935. That was the time William Aberhart put over one of the biggest frauds ever perpetrated on the people of Alberta when he promised them the sum of $25 a month; that is, he promised that to every citizen in Alberta, whether he worked or not, and he did not have to pay it back, either. That promise was made to the people of the province of Alberta in 1935. The leader of the Social Credit party in this house was one of the instigators of that plan at the time, and the people of the province of Alberta fell for it. Those were depression years. Economic conditions were terrible out west, and many of the people said: We will vote Social Credit regardless, as things couldn't be worse. Eventually, as we have found, they changed their tune. They have changed their tactics. There was no dividend and no payment.
The people have not changed. They still vote Social Credit.

Because the people of Alberta thought they were getting a good conservative government. I want to say this. I do not want to compare Conservatives and Social Crediters. I do not want to be disrespectful to the Conservatives because I have a great deal of respect for them, although I disagree with some of their policies. As I say, the Conservative party is one that has had the confidence of the people throughout our


history in Canada, and I hope they continue to have the confidence of the people in the future.
As we have in Alberta.
Just the other day the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) made this statement.
Where is it to be found?

It is reported in Hansard. He made a great many statements, but here is one he made as reported at page 550 of Hansard of December 11:
Social Credit would, through the monetary commission, issue to consumers consumer purchasing power in such forms and in such amounts as might be found needful to equate consumption with production in the nation's economy. That sounds sensible, does it not?
I wonder. To continue:
It cannot be done without debt-free money. Such issues of consumer purchasing power might fittingly be called national dividends.
In other words we are again going back to that same -theory that was propagated in the province of Alberta in 1935. I might point out that since that time some financial experts have come into Alberta. One of them was Mr. Powell. I believe he was sent down by Mr. Douglas, and Mr. Manning was there, too. After he spent some time in Alberta he had to spend the rest of the time in the Alberta jail. After he spent the time in jail he was deported to the old country where he came from. There was still another financial expert who came into Alberta from the old country, Mr. Byrne; and he was fired. The only financial expert I know of right now is the hon. member for Lethbridge. I do not know what will happen to him.
That is about all you need.

I agree with the hon. member. There have been some other new theories developed in Social Credit. The hon. member for Peace River was talking about oil. He said it was fortunate that oil came into the province of Alberta at the time it did. I wonder if he knows how oil did come into the province of Alberta.
Did the Liberals bring it in?

I am sorry I have not the date of this newspaper clipping, but the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) will recall the date. It was when he spoke at the Calgary Social Credit constituency association, at the bible institute, and this is what he had to say:
Mr. Hansell concluded wtih a reference to the Alberta government's financial position, saying other parties claimed that the province was prosperous because of oil having been discovered.

But, said Mr. Hansell, oil was always there. It was discovered under Social Credit and there might be a reason for that. "Perhaps," he said, "even Providence might have said, 'we are not going to place this wealth into the hands of just anybody'."
References have been made to the Social Credit claiming a monopoly on religion. That is not only a monopoly on religion, but the above statement claims a monopoly on the favours which Providence bestows on a government. We have listened to the hon. member for Lethbridge and the hon. member for Peace River telling us what Social Credit is. I say that if you took all these words used by the hon. member for Peace River such as bandit leader, stinkers in high places, cesspool methods, gutter politics, master of smear technique, master of evasion, tommyrot, and put them together, then, Mr. Speaker, you have Social Credit.
The Address-Mr. Decore

Mr. Speaker, since we have had quite a long and hectic day, may I be permitted to move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Roberge the debate was adjourned.
